The verified vendor message is subtract-and-measure, which is the parked feature's optimize-flags-stale-rules spec, not a fetch pipeline. My lens moves Q3 from 'push the guide' to 'audit against the guide'. Q4 — 'in recent sessions I've been getting some slop that took hours and that was not shippable.' This is the only claim in the frame that could justify P0 over the incremental fixes, and it carries no number: no session IDs, no count, no diff, while the repo ships `joycraft telemetry` (src/telemetry.ts). An auditor cannot let an unverified anecdote decide a rebuild. My lens moves Q4 to: produce the telemetry before the panels decide. Q5 — 'insanely good and basically free' — the pack's own §7 concedes routing is the only use with evidence (a 60-char-description cookbook on 'easier than user' requests); the human's enthusiasm is not evidence, and P0 does not need Jev to be true. Condition for P0 to stand: after the incremental set ships (two dirs, disable-model-invocation on the 11 agent-entry skills, folder-map regeneration, the tune path fix, description rewrites) plus one CLI state query that replaces the 10 verified human-glue handoffs, telemetry must still show the unshippable-loop problem at a measured rate. If that residual exists, reimagine; the current pack does not show it.

P1 · 4 skeptics

Hub plus few doors beats 22 commands

qualify
Ruling

P1 does not stand as written. It bundles four mechanisms — an always-loaded router block, a hub skill, forwarding shims, and a door-count cut — and only the router block has measured support. The proposition holds only as: a compact router block in AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md delivered to existing installs by a new idempotent marker patch; the 11 `entry: agent` skills hidden from auto-invocation (disable-model-invocation on Claude, generated agents/openai.yaml on Codex); descriptions rewritten in users' words; and the hub admitted as one thin additional door that reads code-computed state (P2) and forwards, kept alongside the nine human door names rather than replacing them, until `claude plugin eval` and skill-invocation telemetry show a delta. Permanent forwarding shims are rejected; time-boxed, descriptionless shims are allowed on Claude only.

The claim as argued

One hub skill plus a small visible core, with a compact always-loaded router block in AGENTS.md and forwarding shims for old names, beats 22 slash commands. Skeptic angles: compaction loses bootstraps (Superpowers admits it); no study compares entry-point counts for onboarding; gstack and GSD grew despite sprawl; a hub adds a hop before every task.

Replacement claim

A compact always-loaded router block plus hidden internals and user-vocabulary descriptions, delivered to existing installs, beats today's 22 auto-invocable skills; a hub skill is an optional thin door on top, unproven until measured, and does not retire the nine human doors on this evidence.

Condition

All of: (a) the router block ships as an idempotent marker patch into existing AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md, generalizing the model-profile row patch (src/update-inventory.ts:561-592), because materializeDocuments treats both files as create-once (src/update-inventory.ts:236-262) and the ~15 colleagues' installs would otherwise never receive it; (b) the 11 agent-entry skills leave the listing — `disable-model-invocation: true` on Claude, `policy.allow_implicit_invocation: false` in a generated agents/openai.yaml on Codex (frontmatter flag ignored there, openai/codex#29989) — and descriptions are rewritten in the user's vocabulary, since today only joycraft-setup's is; (c) the hub is a thin dispatcher (≤100 lines) over code-computed state, not a prose intent-judge, and it is added as a tenth door while the nine human door names remain the documented vocabulary; it replaces them only after `claude plugin eval` (tool_used grader, Δ vs baseline) and `joycraft telemetry` extended to count Skill tool_use events show that colleagues invoke it and stop invoking the doors; (d) trivial requests bypass the lifecycle — no Superpowers-style "1% chance → MUST invoke" wording, which obra/superpowers#2377 (2026-09-24) reports over-escalating trivial asks on Fable 5.1; (e) shims carry no description on Claude, are omitted or given a dated removal on Pi/Codex/Copilot/omp where they cannot be hidden, and are never permanent — Superpowers deleted exactly this pattern for confusing the model (#756), and BMAD's went opt-in within 25 days.

Judge's reasoning

Four skeptics, four "qualified" verdicts, but with conditions that conflict, so the judge's job was to find what all four agree on and adjudicate the rest. Agreement, all four: (1) the "compaction loses bootstraps" skeptic angle is a misread — Superpowers' README scopes it to Hermes, which lacks a post-compaction hook; Claude Code re-reads CLAUDE.md after /compact and Pi re-injects; so a router block in AGENTS.md is the mechanism that survives compaction, and this angle does not touch P1 as formulated. (2) The "22 compete" premise does not bite in isolation: I recomputed the 22 descriptions at 3,955 chars with the `description:` prefix, 3,619 text-only, 3,647 installed — the skeptics' 3,955/3,655/3,347 are the same numbers counted differently, all 42-49% of the 8,000-char figure, and #64606's own 22-skill project at 2,801 chars was unaffected. The 1% budget and least-invoked-drop-first rule are not on the Claude Code skills page (verified by WebFetch this session); the pack attributes them to the docs, but they come from a user-filed issue closed as not planned. The pressure Joycraft faces is from third-party plugin skills sharing the listing, which a router block outside the listing and disable-model-invocation on internals relieve, and which a 22→8 consolidation alone does not. (3) The Vercel 53→79→100 numbers hold, but the pack drops the authors' caveat that the eval measured one skill's framework-docs retrieval, not routing among workflows, and that skills suit "vertical, action-specific workflows that users explicitly trigger" — a description of Joycraft's doors. (4) No cited source anywhere tests a hub skill: Superpowers has no hub, BMAD cut to eight not one, GSD had a /gsd-next router over 72 commands and is archived. (5) Joycraft already ships a hub-shaped door — joycraft-setup is a pure forwarder to tune with no inbound references and no invocation data. Adjudicated disagreements: on the hub, I side with team-lead and harness-expert (admit it as a thin additional door) over the auditor's outright rejection, because the auditor's verified compaction point — hub body is dropped most-recent-first — is partly defused: a routing hub has finished its job once it forwards, and what is lost is in-flight position, which is P2's oracle, not P1. But I side with the auditor over the novice on shims: the novice's "cheap, BMAD precedent" reading omits that BMAD made shims opt-in on fresh installs 25 days later and that Superpowers deleted its stubs because "Claude is increasingly confused by the old slash commands" with users seeing duplicates (#756). On the count itself, I side with team-lead: the fair comparator is nine human doors plus eleven hidden internals, not 22 commands, and the door names are how a junior learns the lifecycle the maintainer names as the invariant in Q1. The novice's point that question load, not command count, drives Level 1-2 abandonment (tune asks four swarm/model/effort questions per harness at joycraft-tune.md:158-171) is correct and is the reason condition (d) exists, but it is a P2/P11 fix and the novice conceded P1 alone is neutral for that user. Finally, delivery: novice and harness-expert both found that AGENTS.md is create-once, so the always-loaded router — the only measured piece — never reaches existing installs without new machinery; team-lead and auditor did not raise it, but it is decisive for the maintainer's "15 colleagues" frame and becomes condition (a).

Strongest refutation considered

The evidence-auditor's: P1 bundles four claims and only the router block is measured; the hub skill has no cited test in the pack; on Claude Code the hub is the worst-placed artifact because compaction re-attaches invoked skills most-recent-first within 25,000 tokens and "older skills can be dropped entirely" (verified verbatim on code.claude.com/docs/en/skills.md this session), so a session-start hub is the first thing lost; permanent forwarding shims are the exact pattern Superpowers deleted for confusing the model; and the count penalty does not bite at ~45% of budget. I accept the unmeasured-hub and shim points in full. I narrow the compaction point: the router block persists, the hub's body being dropped costs nothing once it has forwarded, and the real loss — where the user is in the lifecycle — is the state-oracle problem P2 addresses. That narrowing is why the ruling is qualify rather than flip.

Human position moved?

Yes, on three points. (1) §0 'Users forget the many slash commands': moved. The forgetting is nine human doors, not 22, and its cause is naming — descriptions are process jargon ('decompose', 'atomic specs', 'deny patterns') and only joycraft-setup speaks in the user's words (pack §8.6, confirmed in frontmatter). A description rewrite plus hiding the 11 agent-only skills fixes it without a hub. The premise is also unmeasured: telemetry.json records doc reads only, though the scanner already sees Skill tool_use events. (2) §0 'all 22 skills compete for auto-invocation': moved. At 3,619-3,955 chars the 22 sit at 42-49% of the 8,000-char figure, below the failure band in #64606 (whose 22-skill project was unaffected). What competes with Joycraft is the hundreds of third-party plugin skills in the maintainer's own sessions; a router block outside the listing and disable-model-invocation on internals relieve that, a 22→8 consolidation alone does not. (3) Q2 'me truly first … if I can get it to work best for me, we can easily get it for others': moved on delivery, not on priority. The super-user routes in his head and gains least from a hub; the fifteen colleagues are existing installs whose AGENTS.md the updater treats as create-once (update-inventory.ts:236-262), so the only measured piece of P1 never reaches them without a new marker-patch kind the intent does not name. 'Works for me → works for others' is therefore a delivery claim that today's updater cannot honor. Not moved but split: Q1 'getting people used to TDD agentic development' — team-lead argues named doors teach the lifecycle and a hub that decides for the junior teaches nothing; novice argues a Level 1-2 user leaves if the word TDD or a failing-test approval appears at all. The panel did not resolve which reading of Q1 the maintainer intends, and P11's background fork is where that lands. Q3 ('push the new prompting guide … everyone gets the new juice') is unaffected by P1.

Skeptic disagreements

  • Hub skill: novice accepts a hub if it infers stage from repo state and drops tune's questions; team-lead admits it only as a tenth door beside the nine named doors; harness-expert demotes it to an optional thin door (≤100 lines) until `claude plugin eval` shows it triggers; evidence-auditor rejects it outright — no cited test anywhere, first artifact dropped at compaction on Claude Code. Three permit under conditions, one rejects.
  • Forwarding shims: novice calls them cheap and mechanically safe (BMAD precedent; update-plan.ts drops vendor skills cleanly); team-lead says they are not free (BMAD went opt-in via --shims in 25 days; Superpowers #756 duplicate-result confusion); harness-expert says net-negative on Pi/Codex/Copilot/omp because disable-model-invocation is Claude-only, so shims add listed descriptions on four of five harnesses; auditor says permanent shims are contradicted by Superpowers' deletion and BMAD's v7 time-box. Novice vs the other three.
  • Compaction: all four agree 'Superpowers admits compaction loses the bootstrap' is Hermes-only and misread, and that a router block in CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md survives /compact. Auditor alone adds that the hub skill body is dropped most-recent-first (verified). Team-lead reframes what is lost as the hub's in-flight position → P2. Compatible but differently weighted.
  • What the 22-description listing competes with: team-lead says Joycraft's 22 at ~48% of budget do not compete at all today; harness-expert says they compete only with third-party plugin skills and consolidating Joycraft does not relieve that — a router block outside the listing and disable-model-invocation do; auditor says the shared budget means fewer Joycraft descriptions do buy headroom. Mild tension on whether consolidation has any budget value.
  • Teaching vs hiding the lifecycle: team-lead argues named doors are how a junior learns the lifecycle and 'a hub that decides for them teaches nothing' (Q1's TDD invariant cuts against hiding steps); novice argues a hub must ask no question that requires knowing the lifecycle and must do TDD silently. Direct conflict over what serves Q1.
  • Number of skills to hide: team-lead hides the 11 agent-entry skills (leaving 9 human + 2 situational visible); auditor hides 13 (agent + situational), leaving 9. Minor.
  • Delivery to existing installs: novice and harness-expert make the create-once AGENTS.md (update-inventory.ts:236-262) a hard condition; team-lead and auditor do not raise it. Omission, not contradiction, but decisive for the '15 colleagues' frame.
  • Superpowers #2377 (over-escalation on Fable 5.1): novice treats it as evidence that an always-routing hub over-routes; harness-expert lists it title-only as unverified; team-lead and auditor do not cite it.
  • Traction evidence: team-lead reads 'every leader that consolidated kept or grew, none reverted' as mild support; auditor reads gstack growing at 43 commands and GSD dying at 52 as 'sprawl vs death uncorrelated'. Both conclude the star counts are uninformative for P1.

What would change the ruling

Toward keep: a `claude plugin eval` run (tool_used grader, 3 runs, Δ vs no-plugin baseline) comparing hub+router against nine doors+router that shows the hub raises correct-skill trigger rate on realistic colleague prompts without over-routing trivial ones; or skill-invocation telemetry across the ~15 colleagues (extend src/telemetry.ts to count Skill tool_use) showing they invoke three or fewer doors and never the rest. Toward flip (router block only, no hub): the same eval showing the hub adds mis-routes or escalates trivial requests, or a reproduction of Superpowers #2377's over-escalation on Fable 5.1 with an always-route hub. Tightening the count argument: official documentation or Claude Code source confirming the listing budget, its sharing with plugin skills, and the drop order — today all three rest on a closed issue. Weakening condition (a): evidence that Codex, Pi, and omp also re-read AGENTS.md after their own compaction, and a shipped marker-patch that reaches existing installs. Any published study varying entry-point count for onboarding — none exists as of 2026-09-24 (pack §4 Unverified; novice's own search found only arXiv 2607.01418, which does not vary count).

Skeptics

Novice vibe coderqualified
Strongest refutation

Command count is not what makes me quit in week two; the questions are. I never type slash commands, so 22 vs 1 is invisible to me; auto-invocation picks. What I see is the first door, and today Joycraft's first door is ALREADY a hub: joycraft-setup is a pure forwarder that says "Run tune" (src/skills/joycraft-setup.md:12-18), the same stub pattern Superpowers deleted. Tune then asks me, per harness, "swarms for decompose? swarms for implement? which model? which effort?" (src/skills/joycraft-tune.md:164-171). I cannot answer one of those. A hub whose invariants are fixed as "gates + lifecycle + TDD loop" (human Q1) inherits the same gates and asks the same questions, so P1 as stated changes nothing for my retention. Worse, the traction precedent the pack leans on cuts against me: Superpowers' hub is 65 lines of "1% chance ... YOU DO NOT HAVE A CHOICE" and, as of today, an open issue (#2377, 2026-09-24) reports it makes Fable 5.1 escalate trivial requests into spec + planning and run for hours with no visible output. For a novice that is the exact failure: ask for a button color, get an interview. A hub that always routes is a hub that over-routes. And the router block in AGENTS.md never reaches the ~15 existing colleagues, because AGENTS.md is create-once (src/update-inventory.ts:238-258), so they get a hub with no router.

Qualification

Hub + few doors beats 22 for a Level 1-2 user only under all three of: (a) the hub asks no question that requires reading a diff or knowing the lifecycle — it infers stage from repo state (P2) and drops tune's swarms/model/effort questions from the first run, offering "I don't know / just do it" as a first-class answer; (b) trivial requests bypass the lifecycle entirely — no Superpowers-style "1% chance → MUST invoke" rule, since #2377 shows that pattern escalating trivial asks on Fable 5.1; (c) the router block and shims reach existing installs, which needs a new AGENTS.md patch kind because AGENTS.md is create-once (update-inventory.ts:238-258). Absent (a), P1 is neutral for my retention; absent (b), it is worse than 22 skills that mostly stay quiet.

Evidence for the refutation

Evidence against it

  • Fewer competing descriptions is a measured gain: all 22 Joycraft skills compete for auto-invocation with none marked disable-model-invocation, and Claude Code silently drops least-invoked descriptions at 25-56 skills (#64606); Vercel saw the skill never invoked in 56% of cases with default behavior. pack §8.6, §4.8; https://vercel.com/blog/agents-md-outperforms-skills-in-our-agent-evals (2026-01-27)
  • One hub description written in my words is easier than 22: today only setup's description uses user language; the rest say 'decompose', 'atomic specs', 'deny patterns', 'bookend' (new-feature.md alone has 21 'spec' and 14 'decompose'). src/skills/*.md frontmatter; grep counts this session
  • Consolidation with shims has a live precedent that kept users: BMAD core cut from fourteen skills to eight, every retired ID resolves through a forwarding shim in v6-shims/ until v7. https://github.com/bmad-code-org/BMAD-METHOD/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md (fetched 2026-09-24)
  • Collapsing skills is mechanically safe today: dropped vendor skills are removed cleanly, edited ones kept as orphans, so shims need no new machinery. src/update-plan.ts:386-399; pack §8.8
  • The hop is invisible to a novice when the hub is auto-invoked; its cost is tokens, not a command I must remember. pack §2.2-2.3 (progressive disclosure, L1 ~100 tokens/skill)

On the human's position

Q1: "getting people used to TDD agentic development as opposed to endless vibe coding (the essence and core objective of joycraft)". From my lens this is the sentence that decides P1, and it is not about command count. I do not know what TDD is. If the hub's fixed invariant surfaces that word, or asks me to approve a failing test I cannot read, I leave in week one whether there is one door or 22. The hub can only keep me if TDD is something it does silently and shows me as "it works / it does not, here is why" in plain words. Q2: "me truly first as I am the super user ... as this system gets much easier house and more driven by the harness this becomes a non issue really". I attack "becomes a non issue" as a hope, not a plan: the maintainer's own pack says the architecture-defense practice "requires a CS background, so it is useless for Joycraft's novice users" (§0), and today's super-user-first door asks about swarms, models, and effort (tune.md:164-171). A hub designed for the super-user first will ask super-user questions first. My lens moves the position: P1 stands for the maintainer and his practitioners (fewer competing descriptions, cheap shims), but it does not stand as a fix for "users forget the many slash commands" among novices, because novices never used the commands. For them P1 only pays off when it is chained to P2 (the hub infers stage from repo state instead of asking) and P11 (the vocabulary fork). Adopt P1 on its own and the novice gets a renamed quiz.

Team lead, five engineersqualified
Strongest refutation

P1 beats a straw man. Joycraft does not present "22 commands" to a developer: the canonical frontmatter declares 9 `entry: human` doors, 11 `entry: agent`, 2 `entry: situational` (src/skills/joycraft-*.md lines 2-6 of each; optimize enforces ≤9 doors at src/skills/joycraft-optimize.md:99-102). The full 22-description listing is 3,955 chars canonical / 3,859 chars installed (`grep -h '^description:' src/skills/*.md | wc -c`), i.e. ~48% of Claude Code's 8,000-char listing budget and under Codex's "2% of context or 8,000 chars" budget — the measured routing failure in claude-code#64606 begins at 25 skills × ~490 chars (153%), and that issue's own 22-skill project (2,801 chars, 35%) was fine. So the count-sensitivity evidence the lead leans on does not bite Joycraft today. The fair comparator for a team is therefore "9 named doors + 11 hidden internals" (disable-model-invocation on Claude; `agents/openai.yaml` `allow_implicit_invocation: false` on Codex, since Codex ignores the frontmatter flag) versus a hub. Against that comparator the hub costs my team the one property named commands give for free: when engineer A on Codex and engineer B on Claude Code type the same door, they run the same skill body. A hub routes by model judgment, and routing quality differs by model and harness (the pack's own Jev cookbook still mis-routed 7.3% with a judge; Scott Spence measured 50–55% auto-load without a hook). Every mis-route is a divergent artifact I review. The "measured fix" cited for the hub — Vercel's 8KB AGENTS.md index at 100% — measured one skill's framework knowledge, not routing among many workflows, and its authors say skills "work better for vertical, action-specific workflows that users explicitly trigger", which is exactly what Joycraft's nine doors are.

Qualification

Hub + few doors beats the current surface only under all three of: (1) the hub is a thin dispatcher over code-computed state (P2's CLI oracle: what exists, what is next), not a prose router that judges intent — so five developers on two harnesses receive the same next step; (2) the nine human-door names stay as the team's canonical, documented vocabulary, with the hub added as a tenth door rather than replacing them behind time-boxed shims — BMAD's shims went from default to opt-in (`--shims`) in 25 days (v6.11.0 2026-08-09 → v6.12.0 2026-09-03) and Superpowers' stubs confused fresh installs (obra/superpowers#756, 2026-03-16) before being deleted; (3) the cheap baseline — hide the 11 agent-only skills on Claude via disable-model-invocation and on Codex via generated agents/openai.yaml, rewrite descriptions in users' words — ships first and the hub is adopted only if `claude plugin eval` (tool_used grader, Δ vs baseline) shows a positive delta. Compaction is not a valid condition: the router block survives because project-root CLAUDE.md is re-read after /compact; what does not survive is the hub's in-flight position, which is again P2.

On the human's position

Section 10 has no direct P1 answer; the closest words are §0 \"Users forget the many slash commands\" and Q2 \"I now have about 15 colleagues all of use it daily driver, across different size teams, but if I can get it to work best for me, we can easily get it for others.\" Two attacks. First, \"many slash commands\" is nine human doors, not 22; the forgetting is a naming problem — descriptions are process jargon and only `joycraft-setup` speaks in the user's words (pack §8.6, src/skills/joycraft-setup.md:6) — and a description rewrite plus hiding the 11 agent-only skills fixes it without touching routing. Second, \"works best for me → works for others\" is the wrong inference for a team: the super-user already routes in his head, so a hub costs him nothing, while its variance cost (different next step per model, per harness, per developer) lands on the five engineers whose output the lead reviews. Q1's own invariant — \"the formality of the loop, getting people used to TDD agentic development\" — cuts against hiding the steps: named doors are how a junior learns the lifecycle; a hub that decides for them teaches nothing. My lens moves the position partway: keep the nine door names as the team's shared vocabulary and teaching aid, add one hub door that answers \"where am I, what is next\" from code-computed state, and do not retire the doors on the evidence in this pack.

Strongest refutation

P1 bundles three mechanisms and only one has evidence. (1) The always-loaded router block is the measured piece — but the evidence is Vercel's 8KB *docs-path index* for Next.js API tasks, whose authors say "Skills work better for vertical, action-specific workflows that users explicitly trigger" (exactly what Joycraft skills are), and Claude Code's docs say CLAUDE.md is what survives compaction ("Put persistent rules in CLAUDE.md rather than relying on conversation history"). So a router in AGENTS.md sidesteps the Superpowers compaction failure; that part stands. (2) The hub skill is unmeasured anywhere: Superpowers (291k) has no hub and no commands; BMAD cut 14→8, not to 1; GSD had a `/gsd-next` router over 72 commands and is archived. Joycraft already ships a hub-shaped door — `src/skills/joycraft-setup.md:1-18` is a pure alias to tune — with zero inbound references and no invocation telemetry (§8.1, §8.6), so the repo's own hub has never been shown to be used. A hub that routes must read state, which makes P1's value contingent on P2; without the oracle it is a menu, and the router block already is the menu. (3) Forwarding shims are net-negative on non-Claude harnesses: `disable-model-invocation` is Claude-only (§2.1), so on Pi/Codex/Copilot 22 shims + hub + core means MORE listed descriptions than today, and BMAD's shims require explicit approval and refuse to start unattended. (4) The premise "22 skills compete" is weak in isolation: the 22 descriptions total 3,655 chars against the 8,000-char default budget (46%); issue #64606's own table shows a 22-skill/2,801-char project at 35% with no loss. The pressure comes from third-party plugin skills in the same listing — which consolidating Joycraft does not fix, and which a router block outside the listing does. (5) Delivery: the updater treats AGENTS.md as create-once (`src/update-inventory.ts:236-262`); the only post-creation edit is the exact model-profile row patch (`src/update-inventory.ts:561-592`). Without new marker-patch machinery the router block never reaches the ~15 existing daily-driver installs the intent names.

Qualification

On the human's position

The maintainer's position on P1 is in the intent's problem statement: colleagues "forget which of the many slash commands to run, and all 22 skills compete for auto-invocation," and in Q2, "Me truly first as I am the super user of this product." My lens moves both halves. On "forget which command": that is a discoverability defect the always-loaded router block and user-vocabulary descriptions fix directly — the pack itself notes only `setup` uses the user's words (§8.6) — and a hub adds nothing to it except a second body to load; Superpowers solved the same complaint by deleting commands, not by adding a hub. On "22 compete": 3,655 chars is 46% of the default budget, so Joycraft's own skills do not compete with each other; they compete with the third-party plugin skills in the maintainer's environment (this session lists hundreds), and consolidating 22→8 does not relieve that — a router block outside the listing and `disable-model-invocation` on the 11 agent-entry skills do. On "me truly first": the super user does not forget the commands; the fifteen colleagues do, and they are existing installs whose AGENTS.md the updater will never rewrite (update-inventory.ts:236-262). If the human wants this to land for them, the deliverable is a marker-patch into existing memory files, which the intent does not name. Net: the human's diagnosis is half right (discoverability) and half misattributed (competition), and the fix they should insist on is router-block-plus-hidden-internals delivered to existing installs, with the hub demoted to an optional thin door until `claude plugin eval` shows it triggers.

Finally, the premise "users forget the slash commands" is unmeasured: docs/.joycraft/telemetry.json holds doc reads for 14 sessions and no skill-invocation counts, although src/telemetry.ts:114 already sees Skill tool_use events.

Qualification

P1 stands only as: (a) a compact always-loaded router block in AGENTS.md (measured: Vercel 100%, Spence 22/22, gstack's routing block) plus (b) `disable-model-invocation` on the 13 agent/situational skills so ~9 doors compete, keeping the current 22 files. It fails as stated for the hub skill (no cited test; first artifact dropped at compaction on Claude Code) and for permanent forwarding shims (Superpowers deleted exactly that pattern for confusing the model; BMAD time-boxed its shims to the v7 cut). Any further collapse of door count should wait for skill-invocation telemetry from the 15 colleagues, since the "users forget" premise has no measurement and the listing-budget penalty does not bite at 3,347 of 8,000 chars.

On the human's position

Q2: "Me truly first as I am the super user of this product, but I now have about 15 colleagues all of use it daily driver… if I can get it to work best for me, we can easily get it for others." A hub is optimized for the user who forgets names; the super-user who knows all 22 is the person a hub hop costs most and helps least, so "works best for me" and P1 pull in opposite directions unless the router block, not the hub, is the thing being shipped. The premise about colleagues forgetting commands is unmeasured: the repo's own scanner (src/telemetry.ts:114) already sees Skill tool_use events but only counts docs. My lens moves the position to a condition: extend `joycraft telemetry` to count skill invocations across the 15 colleagues' transcripts, then collapse whatever the data says nobody invokes. Q1: "the formality of the loop, getting people used to TDD agentic development" — a router block in AGENTS.md preserves that formality after compaction; a hub skill does not, because on Claude Code it is the first invocation dropped. Q3: "push the new prompting guide to an update and everyone gets the new juice" is unaffected by P1 either way.

P2 · 4 skeptics

The CLI as state oracle beats prose handoffs

qualify
Ruling

Code-computed queue/status state beats prose re-derivation, but only as a vendored, manifest-pinned, same-bundle script shipped to all five harnesses (the docs/.joycraft/check.mjs and .pi/scripts/joycraft pattern), never as a runtime `npx joycraft` call; and it removes the pasted briefing's mechanical lines, not the /clear handoffs, which exist for context hygiene and are removed by harness primitives (context: fork, pi -p), not by a state query. Sold as "the CLI" or as closing the Q4 slop gap, P2 is refuted.

The claim as argued

Skills should ask the joycraft CLI what exists and what is next (OpenSpec 1.0 pattern), with queue, status, and gate results computed by code, ending the ten "clear the session, paste this briefing" handoffs where the human is the glue. Skeptic angles: CLI/skill drift; offline and CI use; a CLI that must be installed and current on every machine; Pi's "CLI tools with README" philosophy versus Claude Code's skills-first one.

Replacement claim

A vendored, same-bundle state oracle (one node script, all five harnesses, manifest-pinned, fail-explicit, sole writer of spec status) replaces the prose re-derivation of queue/next/status and fills the computable lines of every handoff briefing; it does not remove the /clear boundary at design-bookend gates, and it does not address the implement-loop quality gap the maintainer named in Q4.

Condition

P2 holds when ALL of: (1) the oracle is a dependency-free node script installed into the project tree (docs/.joycraft/), hashed in the manifest at the same vendorVersion as the skills, reading local files only — never `npx joycraft@latest <cmd>` at skill runtime; (2) it ships for every harness (today PI_SCRIPTS install for 'pi' only, src/bundle-inventory.ts:177, and the omp implement variant says "edit .joycraft-spec-queue.json directly"); (3) it emits versioned `--json` and can never produce a silent false success: a "cannot compute" result is an explicit {ok:false, reason} on stdout, and when injected via Claude Code `!command` it is wrapped so the process exits 0 (a non-zero exit aborts the entire skill and Claude never sees its content — code.claude.com/docs/en/skills.md, fetched 2026-09-24); (4) it is the single writer of spec status (owns both the queue JSON and frontmatter, or frontmatter status is dropped) and the skills delete their prose copy of the next-spec rule so exactly one definition exists; (5) fixture tests cover both compact and pretty-printed manifests (the 95c87a0 class) and a test asserts the oracle's rule equals the rule the skills document; (6) scope is queue, status, next, and the computable briefing lines (Start, Order, Decisions stamped, Execution, Done-when); it may report stored gate results but computing gates is P3's problem; (7) the claim is restated as "removes the paste at mechanical handoffs", not "ends the ten handoffs".

Judge's reasoning

The proposition bundles three claims and the skeptics, independently, split them the same way. (A) Code-computed state beats prose: survives, with caveats. Pi's philosophy supports it (Zechner's "CLI tools with README", verified by three skeptics), OpenSpec 1.0 ships it at scale (verified: "AI queries the CLI for real-time state", 70,234 stars, 1.79M npm/mo), and for a mid-tier model deterministic depends_on resolution is real scaffolding. But the repo's own evidence cuts the other way on urgency: I re-ran the auditor's check and found 0 queue/frontmatter mismatches across 131 queued specs (22 pre-frontmatter May specs have no status field), while the only recorded desync in the repo was produced by the code oracle itself — joycraft-mark-done exited 0, printed success, and changed nothing on a pretty-printed manifest (docs/discoveries/2026-07-27-human-readable-output-style.md:17-40), and joycraft-next-spec reported "Pipeline complete" on an unrun queue (src/templates/pi-scripts/joycraft-next-spec:36-44, fixed 95c87a0). Prose state has held; code state lied once. So the benefit is maintenance and determinism, not repair of a live failure, and the oracle must be built to fail explicitly. (B) "The CLI" as the vehicle: refuted as worded. src/cli.ts:20-262 has zero state-reading commands (update, init, upgrade, migrate, telemetry, check, init-autofix, check-version), so this is greenfield, not a rewire. The CLI is npx-resolved, and this repo spent two of sixteen 0.7.x releases (0.7.6 on 2026-07-29, 0.7.10 on 2026-08-11, CHANGELOG.md:206-214, 298-321) on stale npx-cache behaviour; the one runtime CLI call a skill makes today already carries a five-condition degradation clause (joycraft-session-end.md:145). The maintainer already chose the correct shape for skill-invoked runtime code: docs/.joycraft/check.mjs, a vendor file hashed in the manifest and run at every skill entry with "if missing or fails, continue quietly" (src/bundle-inventory.ts:157; src/bundled-files.ts header). OpenSpec's own troubleshooting documents the drift the CLI shape imports ("an outdated CLI reports everything up to date without ever writing the newer workflows"), and its 50 releases in eight months plus issues #1734/#1807 and learning-app #452 show the coupling cost. (C) "Ends the ten handoffs": refuted. The skills state the reason for /clear as context hygiene ("A fresh session for implementation produces better results. This diagnostic session has context noise", joycraft-bugfix.md:265; same at new-feature.md:514), not missing state. Of the decompose briefing's lines (decompose.md:409-425), Start/Order/Decisions/Execution/Done-when are computable; Hazard is judgment. A fresh context is a harness primitive: Claude Code `context: fork` ("The subagent doesn't see your conversation history", verified by WebFetch) and Pi's `pi -p` per-spec process (implement-loop already exists); Codex, Copilot, and omp have no verified equivalent, so the human stays the glue there whatever the oracle knows. Where a handoff could be removed, Joycraft already removed it without a CLI (implement continues the queue in-conversation, implement.md:145; Pi loop). My WebFetch also settled the fail-quiet/fail-loud dispute: on Claude Code a non-zero exit from `!command` aborts the entire skill invocation, and synced skills never run `!` commands at all, so a fail-loud oracle injected at skill load would make the skill unusable offline or in CI; the oracle must fail explicitly on stdout with exit 0, or be invoked via an agent Bash call as check.mjs is today. Net: the direction stands and is mostly already built on Pi; the mechanism named in P2 is the one component the repo has proven cannot be assumed current, and the promise attached to it is the wrong promise.

Strongest refutation considered

The evidence-auditor's: P2 solves a problem the repo does not show (0 mismatches in every feature since 2026-05-28; prose dual-write has held) with a solution the repo already has (joycraft-next-spec / spec-status / mark-done ship as Pi vendor files and implement-feature.md:42 already prefers them when installed), while the only silent state lie in the repo's history came from the code oracle, not from prose. I verified the mismatch count myself (131 specs, 0 mismatches) and the 2026-07-27 discovery. This nearly justifies a flip to "prose is sufficient for frontier models; port the Pi scripts as maintenance, nothing more." It does not carry the flip because (a) the 0-mismatch result was produced by frontier models on the maintainer's own repo and says nothing about a Qwen-class model on Pi resolving depends_on over a 12-row queue, which is the stated multi-harness audience; (b) two stores with two writers and a prose protocol is exactly the state Zechner's post rejects ("state that the model has to track and update"), and the lifecycle doc names the desync as "the bug this lifecycle exists to kill" even though it has not fired; (c) a fixed, tested, manifest-pinned oracle is net-negative maintenance (one node script replaces ~430 lines of bash plus prose duplicates across five trees). So the refutation strips P2 of urgency and of the "reimagining" framing, but leaves a qualified claim standing.

Human position moved?

The human gave no direct P2 answer in §10; the position lives in the intent ('The CLI answers what exists and what is next so skills stop handing off through the human') and leans on Q3 and Q4. The panel moved it in three places. (1) Mechanism, moved: 'the CLI' becomes a vendored, manifest-pinned script in docs/.joycraft/, installed for all five harnesses, never a runtime npx call. Evidence: src/cli.ts has zero state-reading commands; 0.7.6 and 0.7.10 were both stale-npx releases; joycraft-session-end.md:145 already needs a five-condition fallback for the one runtime CLI call; the maintainer's own check.mjs pattern is the correct shape and works offline; OpenSpec's troubleshooting page admits the stale-CLI drift; the version-check hook is claude-only. Q3's 'push the new prompting guide to an update and everyone gets the new juice' is consistent with this — the update payload is vendored files, and that instinct is right for state code too. (2) Q4, moved: P2 does not close the slop gap. During the slop period queue state was correct (0 mismatches including 2026-09-22-fable-native-sdlc-harness); implement-feature runs specs inline in one conversation with no handoff in the loop; verify-in-loop is unshipped (spec-status-lifecycle.md:23). The gap the human names is loop-end verification (P3/P4 territory), and selling P2 as closing it would misdirect maintainer hours. (3) Promise, moved: 'skills stop handing off through the human' is re-scoped to 'the pasted briefing shrinks to its judgment lines'; the /clear boundary at design-bookend gates stays, because the skills themselves justify it as context hygiene and because on Pi a fresh context is always a new process the human or a driver starts. Not moved: the human's want for code-computed state — every skeptic wants it too, the solo-pi lens more than the human because a mid-tier model reads JSON worse; and Q2 'me first as super-user' is where the risk hides, since the maintainer's warm npx cache and network make an @latest oracle look free while colleagues on fifteen machines pay the drift.

Skeptic disagreements

  • Fail-quiet vs fail-loud: harness-expert condition (b) demands the oracle 'fails loud with non-zero exit — skills carry no else-edit-the-JSON fallback'; solo-pi, evidence-auditor, and the maintainer require fail-quiet degradation to the agent reading the file (the check.mjs pattern). Resolved by my WebFetch: on Claude Code a non-zero `!command` exit aborts the whole skill and hides its content, so fail-loud-by-exit-code is incompatible with offline/CI use there. The reconciliation is 'never a silent success' (explicit {ok:false} on stdout) rather than 'non-zero exit'.
  • Handoff count: solo-pi says the pack's 'ten' holds; harness-expert says 9-10, 'close enough'; evidence-auditor rules it a misread (8 carry the briefing block, 13 carry a /clear instruction). My grep: exactly 10 skills contain the literal 'Run {{clear}} first'; 8 carry the paste-this-briefing block; 15 mention /clear at all. The pack's ten is correct for its literal phrasing; the disagreement is definitional, not a misread.
  • Whether prose state has failed: maintainer says 'prose state handling has already failed in this repo (spec-done exists because queue JSON and frontmatter desynced)'; evidence-auditor says 0 mismatches in 131 specs, prose has held. The repo record supports the auditor: the one recorded desync (2026-07-27) was caused by the mark-done script, not by prose; spec-done was created against a hypothesized failure the lifecycle doc names, not a measured one.
  • Scope of 'gate results computed by code': maintainer excludes it ('gate results depend on the harness's test/eval runner and are P3's problem'); evidence-auditor's condition (e) keeps 'computing queue, status, and gate results' in scope; harness-expert lists 'test exit code' as an input. I side with the maintainer: the oracle may report stored gate outcomes, computing them is P3.
  • Replace vs extend the Pi scripts: maintainer wants one node script that replaces the five bash scripts; harness-expert and solo-pi frame it as extending the existing Pi vendor files to all harnesses ('needs no new ownership kind'). Compatible in effect, different in cost; replacement removes the BSD/GNU sed class of bug (6d0de79).
  • Is the existing oracle honest now: harness-expert says post-fix mark-done verifies the write and next-spec normalizes both layouts ('the oracle can be made honest'); evidence-auditor and solo-pi weight the failure itself; harness-expert's own unverified list notes the bugfix row is still in-review with no end-to-end autonomous-loop verification. Both are true; the fix exists, its loop-level verification does not.
  • Where the Q4 slop happened: solo-pi leaves it unverified whether on Pi or Claude Code; harness-expert and maintainer assert it was inside implement-feature running inline on Claude Code (implement-feature.md:48). The pack's §10 does not say which harness; all agree the oracle does not touch it either way.
  • The Pi-philosophy skeptic angle: all four skeptics agree it is inverted — Zechner endorses CLI tools with READMEs, so Pi is the harness most friendly to P2 and Claude Code (via `!command` abort semantics) is the friction point. Recorded as consensus against the proposition's own framing, not a disagreement.

What would change the ruling

Toward keep (CLI as worded): a demonstration that `npx joycraft@<manifest-pinned version> <query>` resolves from the npm cache with no network on a cold machine and in CI, plus evidence that the ten handoffs are motivated by missing state rather than context hygiene (for example, a rewrite of bugfix.md:265 / new-feature.md:514 that the maintainer endorses, or an A/B showing cold-start agents given the briefing do no better than agents given a state query). Toward flip (prose is enough, drop the oracle): a measurement of a Qwen/Kimi-class model on Pi resolving depends_on over the 12-row fable-native queue with the same 0-error rate frontier models show here; or the vendored oracle failing silently again in an end-to-end autonomous loop after the 2026-07-27 fixes (the bugfix row is still in-review with no loop-level verification). Toward tightening the condition: evidence that Codex, Copilot CLI, or omp cannot run a local script at skill entry (which would make the all-harness requirement unachievable), or telemetry from the ~15 colleague machines showing stale-CLI incidents (or none) in the field.

Skeptics

Solo dev on Pi, open-weight modelqualified
Strongest refutation

P2 bundles two claims and only one survives on Pi. (a) "Queue, status, gate results computed by code" is already how Pi works today: `.pi/scripts/joycraft/joycraft-next-spec`, `joycraft-mark-done`, `joycraft-spec-status`, and the `joycraft-implement-loop` driver compute the queue and advance it with a fresh `pi -p` process per spec (src/templates/pi-scripts/joycraft-implement-loop:13-21). So the proposition is not a change for my lens; it is a description of the installed state. (b) "Ending the ten paste-this-briefing handoffs" does not follow from (a). Pi ships no sub-agents ("Spawn Pi instances via tmux", pi.dev live 2026-09-24), so a fresh context is always a new OS process started by the human or by a shell driver, and the oracle changes nothing about that. The remaining /clear handoffs sit between design-bookend skills (interview→new-feature, design/decide/research→decompose, bugfix→implement, session-end→next) whose briefing carries judgment the CLI cannot compute: "Hazard: <the one known trap>" and "Decisions D1-D7 stamped — do not reopen" (src/skills/joycraft-decompose.md:420-427; joycraft-decide.md:312-318). Worse, what P2 as worded would add is "the joycraft CLI" — `dist/cli.js` is never installed into the project (package.json bin; no skill calls `npx joycraft`), so a runtime `npx joycraft@latest <query>` is a registry-backed, network-dependent process whose version floats independently of the manifest-pinned skills (install-manifest.ts:172 records vendorVersion per installed file; the CLI has no such row). And the repo's own code oracle has already produced the worst failure a state oracle can: next-spec reported "Pipeline complete" on a pretty-printed queue, "the same output a genuinely finished queue produces, so an autonomous loop would exit before running a single spec" (src/templates/pi-scripts/joycraft-next-spec:37-44). On a BYO-key budget, a false oracle costs a whole loop run; a mid-tier model reading a 12-row JSON costs a few hundred tokens.

Qualification

P2 stands only under all of the following: (1) 'the CLI' is a vendor-installed, manifest-pinned, network-free file shipped in the same bundle version as the skills that describe its output — the existing `.pi/scripts/joycraft/*` and `docs/.joycraft/check.mjs` pattern — and it is installed for every harness, not Pi alone (today src/bundle-inventory.ts:177 installs the scripts for 'pi' only and the omp/Codex/Copilot skill variants tell the agent to read JSON by hand); (2) the oracle emits a versioned machine-readable result (`--json` with a schemaVersion, as check.mjs already does) and a missing or failing oracle degrades to the agent reading the file, never to a silent 'complete'; (3) spec status is collapsed to one home before the oracle reads it, or the oracle reads both and reports disagreement as an error; (4) the claim is re-scoped from 'ends the ten handoffs' to 'ends the paste at mechanical handoffs (decide→decompose, research→design, decompose→implement, bugfix→implement) by way of a shell driver that spawns fresh `pi -p` processes' — the design-bookend gates keep the human, and on Pi they must, because there is no in-session fresh context. Under those conditions P2 is the right call for a mid-tier model, and it is mostly already built; it is not a reimagining.

On the human's position

The human never answered P2 directly in §10; the position lives in the intent (docs/intent/2026-09-24-dynamic-joycraft.md:14, 'The CLI answers \"what exists and what is next\" so skills stop handing off through the human') and leans on Q4: 'once they actually get to the implementation loop it's basically sit back and relax and have full confidence… in recent sessions I've been getting some slop that took hours and that was not shippable, we have to close that gap.' From my lens that sentence indicts the wrong thing. On Pi the implementation loop already asks code what is next and advances itself with no human paste; the slop gap is a verification gap (P3's territory, verify-in-loop still unshipped per docs/reference/spec-status-lifecycle.md 'Until verify-in-loop ships, session-end graduates in-review → done directly'), not a state-discovery gap. A more exact oracle would have served the same specs to the same model and produced the same slop. Q2, 'Me truly first as I am the super user,' also hides a cost that only my lens pays: the maintainer runs Claude Code with a warm npx cache and a network, so a registry-backed CLI oracle is invisible to him; for a BYO-key user in a container or on a train, `npx joycraft@latest` per skill step is a hang or a failure, and the fix is the pattern the repo already uses for check.mjs and the Pi scripts — a vendored, manifest-pinned, fail-quiet local file. Q3's 'push the new prompting guide to an update and everyone gets the new juice' is the same instinct and it is right for state code too: ship the oracle in the bundle, not from the registry at run time. So my lens does not move the human off wanting code-computed state — I want it more than he does, because my model is worse at reading JSON — but it moves the mechanism ('the CLI' must mean installed scripts, shipped to all five harnesses, not one) and it removes the promise that the oracle ends the handoffs: on Pi the design-bookend handoffs stay with the human because the human is the gate, and the human's own Q4 says the implement loop is where confidence is missing, which no oracle supplies.

Agent-harness expertqualified
Strongest refutation

P2 bundles three separate claims and only one survives. (1) "Ends the ten clear-and-paste handoffs": false as stated. The handoff exists for a fresh context, not for missing state. Of the seven lines in decompose's canonical briefing (src/skills/joycraft-decompose.md:409-425) code can compute four (Start, Order, Done-when, Execution); "Decisions D1-D7 stamped, do not reopen" is half-computable and "Hazard: the one known trap" is agent judgement. So an oracle removes the paste, not the /clear. What removes the /clear is a harness primitive, not a CLI: `context: fork` on Claude Code (code.claude.com/docs/en/skills, fetched 2026-09-24: "The subagent doesn't see your conversation history") and the fresh `pi -p` process per spec on Pi (decompose.md Pi block, .pi/scripts/joycraft/joycraft-implement-loop). Codex, Copilot and omp have no documented equivalent, so the human stays the glue there whatever the CLI knows. (2) "CLI/skill drift is a hypothetical": Joycraft already runs a code state oracle on Pi and it drifted into the worst failure class in three months. `joycraft-mark-done` exited 0 and printed "marked in-review" while changing nothing on the pretty-printed manifest that decompose itself writes, desyncing queue from frontmatter; `joycraft-next-spec` returned "Pipeline complete" on an unrun queue, which would have ended an autonomous loop before spec 1 (docs/discoveries/2026-07-27-human-readable-output-style.md:17-40; docs/bugfixes/pi-scripts/README.md; commits 95c87a0, 6d0de79, c01c4ae). A silently wrong oracle propagates certainty; a wrong prose briefing gets read and questioned by a frontier model. The skills already carry the two-path drift the oracle creates: "use joycraft-mark-done if .pi/scripts/joycraft/ is installed, else edit .joycraft-spec-queue.json directly" (src/skills/joycraft-implement.md:135,138; joycraft-implement-feature.md:42). (3) "CLI as the vehicle": skills reach the CLI through `npx joycraft@latest` (network plus registry round-trip, ~10 call sites), and the one runtime CLI call a skill makes today already needed a degradation clause: "no npx, package not installed, stale cache without the subcommand, offline — note that in one line and continue" (src/skills/joycraft-session-end.md:145). Every oracle call inherits that clause, so the prose fallback comes back inside every skill and the skill now documents two truths. The OpenSpec precedent the lead leans on shows the same bill downstream: nine skills stamped generatedBy 1.3.1 against CLI 1.13.1, +737/-261 rewrite (the-kind-robots/learning-app#452), and `openspec update` silently resurrecting deliberately deleted skill dirs (CristianPerez06/pinpoint#118).

Qualification

P2 stands only under all of these: (a) the oracle is a vendored, same-bundle script installed for every harness (as .pi/scripts/joycraft/* and docs/.joycraft/check.mjs already are), invoked by relative path, never `npx joycraft@latest`, so skills and oracle cannot skew; (b) it computes state from files already on disk (queue JSON, spec frontmatter, brief decisions, test exit code) with `--json`, no network, and it fails loud with non-zero exit — skills carry no 'else edit the JSON directly' fallback path; (c) it replaces the two-store status system with one authority, or at least is the only writer of both, since the July desync came from two stores and two writers; (d) a test asserts the oracle's rule equals the rule the skills document (next-spec = first todo whose deps are in-review/done); (e) the proposition is restated honestly: it removes the paste, not the /clear. Ending the /clear is a separate design that uses `context: fork` on Claude and the `pi -p` loop on Pi, and is UNVERIFIED as possible on Codex, Copilot and omp. Sold as closing the slop gap (Q4), it is refuted.

On the human's position

The maintainer's Q4 words: "once they actually get to the implementation loop it's basically sit back and relax and have full confidence… in recent sessions I've been getting some slop that took hours and that was not shippable, we have to close that gap." From my lens this is the strongest argument against spending on P2 first: the slop was produced inside implement-feature, which runs specs inline in one conversation (joycraft-implement-feature.md:48) with no human handoff in the loop. A state oracle changes who computes "what is next"; it does not change whether what got built is shippable. Helix's confidence comes from blocking gates in the loop, not from a state query. Q3: "all I have to do is push the new prompting guide to an update and everyone gets the new juice" and Q2: "about 15 colleagues all use it daily driver" — both assume every machine runs a current CLI. Today the version-check hook is installed only for the claude harness (update-inventory.ts:128,267,479,505) and skills call `npx joycraft@latest`, so fifteen machines are fifteen chances for the learning-app #452 shape (skills at one version, CLI at another). My lens moves Q4: P2 is orthogonal to the slop gap and should not be sold as closing it. It does not move Q2/Q3, but it attaches a condition: the oracle must be a vendored script that ships in the same bundle as the skills (the docs/.joycraft/check.mjs and .pi/scripts/joycraft pattern, extended to all five harnesses), not an `@latest` CLI.

Maintainer counting hoursqualified
Strongest refutation

P2 names the wrong component and overstates what it removes. (1) The Joycraft CLI has no state-reading command at all (src/cli.ts:20-262: update, init, upgrade, migrate, telemetry, check, init-autofix, check-version), so this is a greenfield subsystem, not a rewire. (2) The repo already built a code oracle once, as Pi bash scripts (src/templates/pi-scripts/: next-spec 108 lines, mark-done 136, spec-status 47, implement-loop 89), and it cost three fix releases (95c87a0 pretty-printed manifest parsed as "Pipeline complete", 6d0de79 BSD sed, c01c4ae stderr noise), 751 lines of tests in six files, reaches only Pi (src/bundle-inventory.ts:175-180), and still sits beside a prose re-implementation of the same algorithm: joycraft-implement-feature.md:42 "use joycraft-next-spec if installed, else read the queue JSON directly"; joycraft-implement.md:26 restates the rule "this matches what joycraft-next-spec serves". That is CLI/skill drift already shipped, before any CLI oracle exists. (3) The npx-resolved CLI is the one component this repo has proven cannot be assumed current: two of sixteen 0.7.x releases (0.7.6 on 2026-07-29 and 0.7.10 on 2026-08-11, CHANGELOG.md:206-214, 298-321) were spent on stale npx-cache behaviour, and the single runtime CLI call skills make today already carries a five-condition fallback sentence (joycraft-session-end.md:145: "no npx, package not installed, stale cache without the subcommand, offline"). Every oracle call multiplies that sentence across 22 skills times five trees. The precedent the pack leans on documents the same wound: OpenSpec's own troubleshooting says "Instruction files come from the installed CLI, so an outdated CLI reports everything up to date without ever writing the newer workflows", and OpenSpec has shipped 50 releases between v1.0.0 (2026-01-26) and v1.13.2 (2026-09-23) to keep CLI and skills in step. That is the cadence a CLI oracle imports. (4) "Ending the ten handoffs" is wrong on the count: /clear is context hygiene, not state lookup; the briefing at joycraft-decompose.md:418-426 has six lines of which four are computable (picking-up, Decisions, Start/Order, Execution) and two are not (Hazard, Done-when semantics). The oracle shrinks the paste; the human still types /clear and a command at every gate, which the headless vision wants human-paced anyway. Where a handoff can be fully removed, Joycraft already did it without a CLI: implement continues the queue "in this same conversation" (joycraft-implement.md:145) and the Pi loop uses the process boundary (pi-scripts/README.md). (5) The maintainer already chose the opposite shape for the one piece of runtime code skills call: not the CLI but a vendored, dependency-free docs/.joycraft/check.mjs (src/bundle-inventory.ts:157, CHECKER_SOURCE at src/bundled-files.ts:193), hashed in the manifest at the same vendorVersion as the skills, invoked as `node docs/.joycraft/check.mjs check --json` at every skill entry. That is Zechner's "CLI tools with README" pattern executed correctly, and it sidesteps the npx-version problem by construction. P2 survives only if it means that, not `npx joycraft <anything>`.

Qualification

P2 stands only under all of these: (a) the oracle is a vendored, dependency-free node script in the installed tree (docs/.joycraft/, like check.mjs), hashed in the manifest at the same vendorVersion as the skills, reading local files only, never `npx joycraft <cmd>` at skill runtime; (b) one implementation serves all five harnesses and replaces the five Pi bash scripts rather than joining them; (c) skills delete their prose copy of the algorithm (no 'else read the queue JSON directly'), so there is exactly one definition of next/status; (d) the script owns both status homes or frontmatter status is dropped; (e) scope is queue, status, next, and the computable briefing lines only; 'gate results computed by code' is out, because gate results depend on the harness's test/eval runner and are P3's problem. Under (a)-(e) the change is net-negative maintenance (deletes ~430 lines of bash plus prose duplicates). Any version that invokes the npm-resolved CLI at skill runtime is refuted by this repo's own release history.

On the human's position

The human did not answer P2 directly; three of the eight answers touch it. Q3: 'all I have to do is push the new prompting guide to an update and everyone gets the new juice.' That assumes the update channel reaches every machine, and this repo's own history says it is the weak link: 0.7.6 and 0.7.10 were both stale-npx releases, and OpenSpec's troubleshooting page admits 'an outdated CLI reports everything up to date without ever writing the newer workflows.' A CLI oracle makes every skill invocation depend on that channel, so the Q3 hope makes P2's drift risk larger, not smaller. My lens moves this: the update payload should be vendored files hashed in the manifest (as check.mjs already is), never a runtime `npx joycraft` call. Q4: 'once they actually get to the implementation loop it's basically sit back and relax... in recent sessions I've been getting some slop that took hours.' The oracle does not touch that gap. On Claude Code the implement loop already runs the queue in one conversation with no handoff (joycraft-implement.md:145); the handoffs a CLI would shrink sit between gates, where the headless vision deliberately keeps the human. Spending maintainer hours there buys nothing against the slop. Q2: 'about 15 colleagues all of use it daily driver, across different size teams.' Fifteen machines means fifteen npx caches; a local vendored script has one version per repo checkout, the CLI has one per machine. Net: my lens does not flip the human toward prose; it moves the human off 'CLI' toward 'vendored oracle script in the installed tree, one implementation for five harnesses, prose fallbacks deleted.'

Qualification

P2 stands only if (a) the oracle is an installed, version-locked repo file shipped in the same update transaction as the skills — not a globally installed or npx-fetched CLI — so it works offline and in CI and cannot drift from the skill text (OpenSpec couples them at `openspec update`; Joycraft's docs/.joycraft/check.mjs and .pi/scripts/joycraft already do this); (b) it is installed for every harness, not Pi-only as today (bundle-inventory.ts:177); (c) every skill call to it carries a fail-quiet fallback, because on Claude Code a failed !`cmd` aborts the skill and hooks fail open; (d) it has fixture tests for both manifest layouts (the 95c87a0 class of silent 'Pipeline complete'); and (e) it is scoped to what it can do — computing queue, status, and gate results — and not credited with ending the /clear handoffs, which are context-hygiene choices solved by `context: fork` subagents or `pi -p` process boundaries, not by state queries.

On the human's position

Section 10 has no direct P2 answer; the nearest words are Q4: "once they actually get to the implementation loop it's basically sit back and relax and have full confidence of when that loop is done they have shippable product... in recent sessions I've been getting some slop that took hours and that was not shippable, we have to close that gap", and the intent's line "The CLI answers 'what exists and what is next' so skills stop handing off through the human." The evidence separates these two. During the slop sessions the queue state was correct — 0 queue/frontmatter mismatches in every feature since 2026-05-28, including 2026-09-22-fable-native-sdlc-harness — so the loop knew what was next and still produced unshippable output. The gap the human names is loop-end quality (P3, gates), not state knowledge (P2). The human also already has the oracle they are asking for: joycraft-next-spec ships to Pi, and the Claude skill only falls back to prose because the script is a Pi-only vendor file. My lens moves the position from "build a CLI state oracle" to "port the existing scripts to an installed, harness-neutral file (like docs/.joycraft/check.mjs), version-locked with the skills, tested against pretty-printed and compact manifests, fail-quiet on Claude Code" — and it strips P2 of the claim that it ends the /clear handoffs, which exist for context hygiene the human's own skills state (bugfix.md:265). Condition for P2 to stand: the oracle is an installed repo file that ships in the same update transaction as the skills (OpenSpec's generation-time coupling, Joycraft's check.mjs pattern), works offline with no npx, and every skill call carries the same 'if missing or failing, continue quietly' clause the check.mjs header already uses. Without that condition, the OpenSpec issues #1734/#1807 and the 95c87a0 bug show a lying oracle is worse than the prose it replaces.

P3 · 4 skeptics

Gates over advice

qualify
Ruling

P3 survives as its Helix sentence ("an attempt may be wrong but cannot ship until it is not") and fails as its stated medium and guarantee: vendor hooks cannot deliver "cannot be overridden" (PreToolUse fails open on timeout in Claude Code and Codex, Stop is capped at 8 consecutive blocks, hook registration is agent-editable here, and Joycraft's only blocking hook was a silent no-op for six months), and the motivating slop is green-but-unshippable output that no deterministic check can see, so the invariant belongs at the status/merge boundary (required CI, a validation precondition on the done transition, an exit-code step in the Pi loop driver) plus a wired fresh-context verifier reading an oracle the agent did not author — with hooks as a pre-filter, every gate contract-tested and fire/false-positive measured, and process prose kept beside gates for sub-frontier execution profiles.

The claim as argued

Process prose should convert to deterministic checks and blocking hooks (Helix: an attempt may be wrong but cannot ship until it is not), with the goal that when the implement loop ends the human can trust the output is shippable. Skeptic angles: hooks are per-vendor with no shared standard; Claude Code and Codex hooks fail open on timeout; Stop hooks may not block at all; false positives block flow; Ronacher's warning that each added defense makes the system less understandable while appearing more robust.

Replacement claim

Gates over advice, restated: rules that are mechanically checkable convert to fail-closed deterministic checks in the CLI/CI exit-code path (not primarily vendor hooks), each shipped with a host-faithful contract test and a measured false-positive rate; the shippability invariant — nothing graduates in-review→done or opens a PR without a required CI check outside the agent's process and an independent fresh-context verifier verdict on an oracle the agent did not author — is the one non-overridable gate; hooks are a pre-filter; process prose stays beside the gates for sub-frontier models. "Sit back and relax when the loop ends" is replaced by Helix's real contract: small checkpoints with per-checkpoint human approval where no reference oracle exists.

Condition

P3 holds only under all of: (1) the invariant is enforced where the gated agent cannot reach it — required status checks on main (tests + typecheck + STE lint; today `required_checks: []`), a validation precondition on `joycraft-mark-done --to done` / the in-review→done transition, and on Pi a test/exit-code step in `joycraft-implement-loop` between implement and spec-done (today lines 79–88 run none); (2) an independent fresh-context verifier is actually wired as the in-review→done gate (verify has zero inbound references; session-end.md:138 still says "Once verify-in-loop ships") and reads an oracle the agent did not author in the same run (held-out or locked tests, CI on the branch, a reference where one exists); (3) vendor hooks are a fast pre-filter only, never the guarantee — PreToolUse fails open on timeout (Claude Code verbatim, Codex by inference), Stop blocks but is capped at 8 consecutive blocks, `.claude/settings.json` is not on the deny list, and only Pi `tool_call` fails closed; (4) every gate ships with a contract test that drives it exactly as the host does (stdin JSON, real timeout) and runs warn-only until its fire rate and false-positive rate are measured over real sessions, then promotes to exit 2; (5) process prose is added-beside, not deleted, for execution profiles below frontier tier (the AGENTS.md profile line already names the model per harness); (6) a failure analysis of the slop sessions precedes choosing which checks to build — none exists in docs/discoveries, docs/context, or docs/intent. Without (1), (2) and (6) the claim is the six-month no-op again: a gate that appears robust, blocks nothing, and retires vigilance.

Judge's reasoning

All four skeptics returned "qualified" and none argued the inverse (advice over gates); the panel's disagreement is about where the gate lives and what it reads, not whether gates beat prose where a rule is mechanically checkable. The deterministic-beats-prose half of P3 has repo evidence in its favor: the docs-sync gate has held on every product PR since it shipped (PRs 73–79 all touched CHANGELOG.md; only #72, the gate's own PR, used the opt-out), harden.md:13 already states the doctrine, and Scott Spence's model-free forced-eval hook went 22/22 with zero false positives. So a flip is unwarranted. A keep is impossible because three independent facts, two of which I verified myself, break the strong form. First, the medium: the live Claude Code hooks doc says a timed-out PreToolUse command/http/mcp_tool hook "doesn't block the tool call... don't count on a stalled hook to act as a gate"; Stop hooks do block (the pack's §2.10 sentence is a misread — I confirmed the phrase does not exist on the page; line 3670 is about async hooks) but line 2552 caps them: "Claude Code overrides the hook and ends the turn after 8 consecutive blocks"; and this repo's deny list has no Edit(.claude/settings.json) entry, so the agent can edit hook registration mid-session. Only Pi's tool_call fails closed, and Joycraft writes no enforcement surface for Pi/Codex/omp today (harden.md:25-29). Second, the repo's own record: block-dangerous.sh read $1, which Claude Code never passes, from 73bfd3f (2026-03-24) to 06f08a8 (2026-09-23) — six months in every install, with a green test that encoded the same wrong contract; pr-docs-gate.mjs needed a false-positive fix 2 minutes 40 seconds after it shipped (e52c1c7 22:44:40 → 8e90c8a 22:46:40). That is Ronacher's warning measured in this codebase regardless of which reading of his paragraph one takes. Third, the target: the slop the maintainer names passed every deterministic gate Joycraft already has (implement.md:105 blocks until criteria are green; session-end step 2 is mandatory and non-overridable in prose), and the agent authors what any gate reads — ImpossibleBench puts frontier cheating near 50% on spec-test conflicts and the DGM deleted its detector's markers. Helix's confidence does not come from determinism: three of its four gates are Gemini review, two context-isolated reviewers, and per-checkpoint engineer approval, and gates 1–2 compare against an existing reference app that greenfield Joycraft specs lack. The verifier Joycraft designed for this (verify-in-loop, 2026-05-28) is unwired. One fact I added: branch protection on main has zero required status checks (one review, admins not enforced), so even the "merge boundary outside the agent's process" that the harness-expert leans on does not exist yet — CI runs tests on PRs but nothing blocks the merge. That strengthens the qualification: the fail-closed boundary must be built, not assumed. On the prose-cut half bundled into P3, the solo-pi lens is right that the ablation paper (2609.20804) shows planning scaffolding helps weaker models, and the ai-researcher is right that it measured no verification axis, so "convert" must mean add-beside for sub-frontier profiles. Finally the position is in tension with the maintainer's own D2 stamped one day earlier ("No continuation logic and no Stop-hook recipe... test whether the standing instruction is enough first"); the panel did not create that tension but it should be resolved before any Stop-gate design.

Strongest refutation considered

The ai-researcher's oracle-authorship argument, combined with the harness-expert's observation that the slop already passed Joycraft's deterministic gates: in the implement loop the gated agent writes the tests, the diff, the commit, and the progress claim, so a deterministic check reads an input the agent controls; ImpossibleBench measures ~50% cheating by frontier models when a visible test conflicts with the spec, monitors catch under half, and the DGM removed the markers its hallucination check depended on. If accepted in full this would flip P3 to "verifiers over gates". I did not flip because the same paper shows the fix is deterministic-shaped — hiding or read-only tests drop cheating to near zero — and because Joycraft's mechanically checkable rules (CHANGELOG touched, deny-pattern grep, test exit codes under test-file-lock) demonstrably hold where prose did not. The argument therefore narrows P3 to gates on oracles the agent cannot author plus one independent verifier, rather than refuting it.

Human position moved?

Yes — Q4 moved on three counts, each with evidence the maintainer did not have. (1) Mechanism: 'Gates that cannot be overridden' is not a property any Joycraft host sells. Live Claude Code docs: a timed-out PreToolUse hook 'doesn't block the tool call... don't count on a stalled hook to act as a gate'; Stop hooks block but Claude Code 'overrides the hook and ends the turn after 8 consecutive blocks' (line 2552, verified by judge); Codex continues the tool call on hook error; only Pi tool_call fails closed. In this repo the agent can edit .claude/settings.json (not on the deny list), write the 'Docs: none' opt-out, and rm the test-lock sentinel; the one blocking hook Joycraft ships blocked nothing from 2026-03-24 to 2026-09-23 with a green test; and branch protection on main has zero required status checks, so the merge boundary that could be non-overridable is not configured either. (2) Target: the position assumes the slop got past advisory prose, but implement.md:105 and session-end step 2 are already non-overridable in wording and the slop passed them (or the validation gate was never reached — no failure analysis exists to say which). Green-but-unshippable is a semantic failure; the gate that sees it is Helix's — an oracle the agent did not author, two context-isolated reviewers, and an engineer — and Joycraft's version (verify-in-loop, designed 2026-05-28) has never been wired (session-end.md:138). (3) Reading of Helix: 'sit back and relax and have full confidence when that loop is done' is not what the source describes. Gate 4 is 'The engineer looks at the code and running app and decides whether the result matches their expectations' at every checkpoint, and checkpoints are 'the screen skeleton' then 'one deliberately small section'; gates 1–2 diff against an existing reference app that a greenfield spec lacks. 'We are already doing a lot of what Helix is doing' holds for the tests gate and fails for the three judgment gates. What did not move: the goal sentence — an attempt may be wrong but cannot ship until it is not — and Q1's 'gates + lifecycle + artifacts fixed' both survive; the panel replaced the vehicle (hooks) with the status/merge boundary plus a wired verifier, and replaced 'sit back' with small checkpoints. One further move the panel surfaced rather than caused: Q4 contradicts the maintainer's own D2 stamped 2026-09-23 ('No continuation logic and no Stop-hook recipe... test whether the standing instruction is enough first'); Q3 parks that feature, but the two rulings should be reconciled before any completion gate is designed. Q1's 'process prose generated' half took a partial hit outside P3's core: two papers say the prose is what mid-tier and open-weight profiles need, so 'generated' must not mean 'deleted' for the colleagues on those tiers.
