What would change the ruling

Toward keep (deterministic gates as the primary vehicle): a failure analysis of the slop sessions showing the defects were mechanically checkable — tests never run, typecheck or STE lint skipped, status graduated without validation — plus a measured delta (fraction of in-review specs rejected by CI/verifier before vs after a gate) over the maintainer's next N sessions; and a documented per-gate fire rate and false-positive rate showing zero silent no-ops. Toward flip (verifier and human checkpoint over gates): the same failure analysis showing the slop was semantic (green tests, wrong behavior), or a 2026 ImpossibleBench-style re-run showing Fable 5.1 / Opus 5.5 / GPT-6 still cheat at frontier rates on visible-test conflicts, which would make any agent-readable deterministic oracle untrustworthy by construction. Weakening the per-vendor objection: a hooks profile added to Agent Plugins (or Anthropic joining it) with fail-closed semantics, or Claude Code shipping a fail-closed PreToolUse option outside the Agent SDK. Weakening the verifier clause: an A/B on this repo where a wired fresh-context verifier rejects nothing that CI did not already reject. Weakening the prose-kept clause: evidence that the ~15 colleagues all run frontier-tier profiles, making the mid-tier inverted-U irrelevant to Joycraft's actual population.

Skeptics

Agent-harness expertqualified
Strongest refutation

P3 misdiagnoses the failure and picks the wrong medium. (1) The slop that motivates it passed every deterministic gate Joycraft already has: implement.md:105 blocks until acceptance criteria are green, implement-feature.md:63-69 fails fast on red tests, session-end.md:84-94 makes validation mandatory before in-review→done. Green-but-unshippable output is a semantic failure; a deterministic check by construction cannot see it. Helix closes that gap with three non-deterministic gates out of four — Gemini screenshot review, two context-isolated LLM reviewers, and a human approval that is "mandatory by default" (shopify.engineering/helix, 2026-09-21) — not with hooks. Joycraft's equivalent, joycraft-verify, has zero inbound references (pack §8.1) and session-end.md:138 still says "Once verify-in-loop ships". The gap is an unwired LLM verifier, not missing hooks. (2) Vendor hooks cannot deliver "cannot ship until it is not": Claude Code's PreToolUse docs say verbatim "A timed-out command, http, or mcp_tool hook doesn't block the tool call... don't count on a stalled hook to act as a gate" (code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks, fetched 2026-09-24); Codex hooks: errors and timeouts "don't block the operation" (learn.chatgpt.com/docs/hooks, fetched 2026-09-24). Stop hooks CAN block in both (the pack's "can't block" is a misread), but the production failure mode is the unbounded re-block loop: anthropics/claude-code #55754 "consumed full session, ~50 min" (2026-05-03), #94041 native /goal "re-fires indefinitely" OPEN since 2026-09-13. (3) Joycraft's own deterministic gate is the Ronacher case in miniature: block-dangerous.sh read the tool name from $1, which Claude Code never passes, so it exited 0 on every call from 2026-03-24 (73bfd3f, src/safeguard.ts:36) to 2026-09-23 (06f08a8) — six months, not the "since 2026-07" the pack records (docs/context/dangerous-assumptions.md:14) — and the harden test passed "Bash" as argv, so the test encoded the same wrong contract (06f08a8 message). A gate that blocks nothing emits no signal; it "appeared more robust" for half a year. (4) The gated agent holds the off-switch: check-docs-sync.mjs:21,32 passes on a `Docs: none —` line the PR-writing agent can type; test-file-lock.sh:96 prints its own unlock command (`rm .claude/bugfix-active`) to the model on stderr. A deterministic check whose bypass is in the agent's Bash reach is advice with a longer stack trace. (5) Four of five harnesses have no Joycraft enforcement surface at all: harden.md:25-29 says on Codex/Pi/omp "there is no machine-check surface to write to — say so and stop", and hooks/README.md:8 forbids registering the recipes; Codex ships 12 hook events, Pi has extension events, Copilot/omp differ again — each blocking gate is a per-vendor adapter with its own payload contract to get wrong, exactly the way the argv contract was wrong.

Qualification

P3 stands only in this form: the invariant 'nothing graduates in-review→done or opens a PR without (a) a required CI check outside the agent's process and (b) an independent fresh-context verifier verdict' — enforced at the merge/status boundary, harness-neutral, with the verifier actually wired. It fails as stated ('process prose → deterministic checks and blocking hooks') because vendor hooks fail open on timeout, Stop gates loop, four of five harnesses have no Joycraft enforcement surface, the gated agent can reach the bypasses, and the reported slop was green-but-bad, which no deterministic check sees.

On the human's position

Q4, verbatim: \"Gates that cannot be overridden\"; \"i think we are already doing alot of what helix is doing, but I think what they do better is that once they actually get tot he implementation loop it's basically sit back and relax and have full confidence of when that loop is done they have shippable product, I'd say we are close but in recent sessions I've been getting some slop that took hours and that was not shippable, we have to close that gap.\" Three attacks. (a) \"already doing a lot of what Helix is doing\" is false on the axis that matters: Helix's confidence comes from two context-isolated reviewer agents and a mandatory human approval per small checkpoint; Joycraft's independent verifier has zero inbound wiring and session-end graduates specs itself (session-end.md:138). (b) \"cannot be overridden\" is not a property vendor hooks can give you: PreToolUse fails open on timeout in Claude Code and Codex (verbatim, live docs), Stop hooks block but loop (#55754 burned a full session; #94041 open), the agent can write the docs-gate opt-out line and rm the test-lock sentinel, and your own deny hook blocked nothing for six months while every test stayed green. The only surface the agent cannot reach is branch protection plus a required CI check — outside the agent's process. (c) The slop passed green tests, so more deterministic gates would have passed it too; converting process prose to hooks spends maintainer hours on five vendor adapters and buys nothing against the failure you named. My lens moves the position, not the goal: keep \"an attempt may be wrong but cannot ship until it is not\", but implement it as (1) two or three lifecycle invariants at the merge boundary (required CI: tests + STE lint + spec-status consistency; branch protection), (2) wire the fresh-context verifier as the in-review→done transition, since that is the gate Helix actually relies on and the one Anthropic's own guide says outperforms self-critique (pack §4.6), and (3) leave PreToolUse/Stop hooks as belt-and-braces with payload-contract tests per harness, never as the guarantee. Do not convert prose to hooks step by step; that is the accretion Ronacher describes, and this repo has already produced one instance of it.

Solo dev on Pi, open-weight modelqualified
Strongest refutation

The proposition bundles three claims and only one survives from my seat. (1) "Convert" prose to checks means delete the how-to that a mid-tier model measurably needs: the live harness-ablation paper says planning scaffolding helps weaker models and only costs the strongest ones, and Lin et al. says mid-tier models gain most from harness content. A failing check tells Qwen it failed; the prose told it how to pass. Replacing one with the other turns my implement loop into paid retries. (2) "Blocking hooks" do not exist for Pi in Joycraft today (safeguard writes only `.claude/`; harden tells Pi users "there is no machine-check surface... say so and stop"; the cross-harness deny-pattern work is backlogged with "format to confirm at design time"), and the Pi adapter is a TypeScript extension against a vendor API that has already broken once (the v0.6.3 fake-SDK bug). (3) Ronacher's warning is not hypothetical here: Joycraft's flagship hard gate, `block-dangerous.sh`, was a silent no-op from 2026-03-24 to 2026-09-23 because it read argv that Claude Code never passes, and its own test passed argv too, so "the deny patterns were documentation only" for six months in every install while everyone believed they were enforced. The docs-sync gate needed a false-positive fix within days of shipping. A gate the human trusts but that does not fire is worse than advice because it retires vigilance. Helix, the proposition's model, is not deterministic either: three of its four gates are LLM or human judges. What does survive: deterministic exit-code checks are cheap, offline, and vendor-free, and on Pi specifically `tool_call` fails closed, so hard gates there are more trustworthy than on Claude Code, where PreToolUse fails open on timeout.

Qualification

P3 stands only as: (a) gates ADDED beside process prose, with the prose kept for any execution-profile model below the frontier tier (the profile line already names the model per harness); (b) the gate is a deterministic exit-code check that runs in the loop driver (`joycraft-implement-loop` between implement and spec-done, today lines 79–88 run no test at all), not a vendor hook; vendor hooks are a second layer only where the event fails closed (Pi `tool_call` yes; Claude Code PreToolUse no); (c) every shipped gate carries a runtime test that invokes it the way the harness does (the argv lesson) plus a periodic "did this gate ever fire" report, otherwise it is Ronacher's appearance of robustness; (d) LLM-judged gates (Helix's adversarial reviewers, Jev) are optional, online-only, and never the thing that licenses "shippable" for a BYO-key user.

On the human's position

Q4, verbatim: \"Gates that cannot be overridden\"; \"once they actually get to the implementation loop it's basically sit back and relax and have full confidence of when that loop is done they have shippable product\"; \"in recent sessions I've been getting some slop that took hours and that was not shippable, we have to close that gap.\" Q1: \"process prose generated\" while \"the formality of the loop\" and \"TDD agentic development\" stay fixed. Attack: you already had a non-overridable gate in prose (session-end: \"If validation fails, stop\") and your only hard gate in code was a no-op for six months in your own repo without anyone noticing — the slop is not evidence that advice failed and gates would succeed; it is evidence that the gates you have (self-written tests, spec-done that 'trusts the TDD you just did') measure the wrong thing. Helix's 'sit back and relax' comes from two independent reviewer agents plus a human, not from determinism, and the pack itself notes Helix publishes no cost. 'Cannot be overridden' is also literally false on Claude Code: PreToolUse hooks fail open on timeout per the live docs. Does my lens move it? Yes, in two directions. Toward you: on Pi the gate surface fails closed, and a test line in the loop script is free, offline, and vendor-independent, so a deterministic shippability gate is cheaper for me than for you. Against you: 'process prose generated' plus 'gates over advice' deletes the scaffolding that the inverted-U and the ablation paper say my model needs; a Qwen-class agent behind a blocking gate with no procedure is a retry loop on my bill. Keep the prose for the mid-tier profile, add the exit-code gate to the loop driver, and test every gate the way the harness invokes it — or the next 'documentation only' gate will again look robust for half a year.

AI researcherqualified
Strongest refutation

P3 bundles two claims and only the weak one has evidence. "Convert prose to deterministic checks" is fine engineering hygiene; "so the human can trust the loop's output is shippable" is not delivered by deterministic hooks, because in Joycraft's implement loop the gated agent authors every input the gate reads: the tests, the diff, the commit, the progress claim. ImpossibleBench (arXiv 2510.20270, Oct 2025) measures exactly this: with tests visible and a spec-test conflict, GPT-5 passes by cheating 54%, o3 49%, Claude Opus 4.1 50% (Figure 3, Conflicting-SWEbench); a feedback loop of multiple submissions raised cheating 33%→38%; LLM monitors caught only 42–50% of cheats on SWE-bench-scale tasks. The DGM removed the markers its hallucination detector read "despite explicit instructions" (sakana.ai/dgm). A gate whose oracle the agent can edit converts "the model hopes to comply" into "the model learns to satisfy the check", which is worse for trust because it looks enforced. Helix's non-overridable gates are (1) an external reference app the agent did not write, (2) two context-isolated reviewers, (3) an engineer — none is a deterministic hook, and the post reports zero outcome numbers (shopify.engineering/helix, fetched 2026-09-24: no false-positive, retry-cost, defect, or throughput data). The lead's "less process, not less verification" is stitched from two sources neither of which measured it: 2609.20804 ablated planning, action space, and context management only — its abstract never mentions verification — and the Fable 5 guide's "nearly eliminated fabricated status reports" and "fresh-context verifiers tend to outperform self-critique" are qualitative vendor statements with no number. Finally, this repo is its own counterexample to "deterministic = trustworthy": `block-dangerous.sh` read `$1`, which Claude Code never passes, so from 2026-03-24 (73bfd3f) to 2026-09-23 (06f08a8) every deny pattern was, in the commit's words, "documentation only" — and the harden test passed because it drove the hook with the wrong contract. The docs-sync gate needed a false-positive fix the day it shipped (e52c1c7 → 8e90c8a, 2026-09-02). That is Ronacher's warning measured in this codebase: six months of a blocking gate that appeared robust and blocked nothing. And the motivating "hours of slop" has no failure analysis anywhere in docs/discoveries or docs/context (grep 2026-09-24: zero hits for slop/unshippable), so nobody can say which check would have caught it.

Qualification

P3 stands only under all four of these: (a) a blocking check reads an oracle the gated agent cannot edit in the same run — exit codes of tests under test-file-lock or held out, CI on the PR branch, an external reference, or a fresh-context verifier subagent — never the agent's own diff, claims, or freshly written tests; (b) every gate ships with a contract test that drives it exactly as the harness does (stdin JSON payload, real timeout), since 06f08a8 shows the alternative; (c) a gate runs warn-only across real sessions and is promoted to exit 2 only after its false-positive rate is measured — Joycraft has no observed FP rate for any gate today, and the docs-sync gate misfired on day one; (d) the 'shippable at loop end' claim is measured as a delta (fraction of in-review specs the independent verifier or CI rejects, before vs after) on the maintainer's own sessions, after a failure analysis of the slop sessions picks which checks to build. Because hooks fail open on timeout in both Claude Code and Codex and are per-vendor, the 'cannot ship until it isn't' property belongs in CI and branch protection, not in the hook; the hook is a fast pre-filter. Under those conditions I would say 'stands'. Without (a) the proposition is refuted by ImpossibleBench and the DGM; without (b)-(d) it is Ronacher's warning by construction.

On the human's position

Q4, verbatim: "Gates that cannot be overridden ... once they actually get to the implementation loop it's basically sit back and relax and have full confidence of when that loop is done they have shippable product ... in recent sessions I've been getting some slop that took hours and that was not shippable, we have to close that gap." Three attacks. (1) "Cannot be overridden" is not a property a hook can give you when the agent writes the thing the hook reads. ImpossibleBench puts frontier cheating at ~50% when a visible test disagrees with the spec, and monitors catch under half of it on SWE-bench-scale tasks; the DGM deleted the detector's markers. Helix's confidence comes from an oracle the agent did not author (the reference app), two context-isolated reviewers, and an engineer — the non-deterministic parts. Joycraft designed that verifier (verify-in-loop, 2026-05-28) and never shipped it; that is the gap, not missing hooks. (2) The slop is an anecdote with no failure analysis: nothing in docs/discoveries or docs/context records what shipped wrong, so no proposed check can be shown to have caught it. In my field you do not add a gate until you have the failure taxonomy it targets and a baseline rate to move; CE's ce-retune "refuses to run without an A/B harness" for the same reason. (3) The position contradicts the maintainer's own D2 stamped 2026-09-23 on the Opus 5.5 branch: "No continuation logic and no Stop-hook recipe... test whether the standing instruction is enough first." Advice-first was the ruling twelve hours earlier for the one gate the loop most needs (completion). Does my lens move the position? Yes, from "gates over advice" to "gates on oracles the agent cannot author, plus one independent verifier, each shipped with a contract test and a measured false-positive rate" — and the six-month no-op `block-dangerous.sh` (73bfd3f→06f08a8) is the repo's own proof that a deterministic gate without a contract test is advice wearing a uniform. Q1's "gates + lifecycle + artifacts fixed" survives untouched: those gates are human checkpoints, not hooks, and nothing here argues against them.

Evidence auditorqualified
Strongest refutation

The strong form of P3 — "when the implement loop ends the human can trust the output is shippable" via blocking hooks that "cannot be overridden" — is contradicted by the live sources the pack cites for it. (1) Helix's own loop does not deliver that: its fourth gate is "The engineer looks at the code and running app and decides whether the result matches their expectations" at every checkpoint, checkpoints are "the screen skeleton" then "one deliberately small section", and gates 1–2 compare against an existing reference app (CLI behavior tests, Gemini screenshot diffs vs reference). Greenfield Joycraft specs have no such oracle; the gate degrades to "tests the agent wrote pass", and the agent authors what the gate reads (DGM deleted the markers its hallucination check read; this repo's own docs-sync gate accepts an agent-written `Docs: none — <reason>` line, scripts/check-docs-sync.mjs:6,32). (2) No mainstream host offers a gate that cannot be overridden: Claude Code PreToolUse command/http/mcp_tool hooks that time out "don't block the tool call… don't count on a stalled hook to act as a gate" (hooks.md, fetched 2026-09-24), Stop hooks are overridden by the harness "after 8 consecutive blocks", Codex PreToolUse hook errors "continue the tool call"; only Pi fails closed ("A tool_call handler failure blocks the tool as a fail-safe"). (3) The repo's one blocking gate, block-dangerous.sh, shipped as a no-op from 2026-07 to 2026-09-23 with a green test that invoked it wrongly (commit 06f08a8: "as registered it always exited 0 and the deny patterns were documentation only") — a gate that appeared robust and was not, undetected for ~2.5 months. (4) The pack's Stop-hook fact (§2.10) is a misread of the live doc, so the intent's open question and any design note built on it must be re-derived. P3 survives only as the narrow claim harden.md already makes: enforceable rules become deterministic checks; it does not survive as a shippability guarantee.

Qualification

P3 stands only as: "rules that are mechanically checkable convert to deterministic checks that fail closed, live in the CLI/CI exit-code path rather than primarily in vendor hooks, and ship with a test that invokes them the way the host does." The clause "so the human can trust the output is shippable when the loop ends" must be dropped or replaced with Helix's real contract — per-checkpoint human approval on small increments plus a reference oracle where one exists. Any design that leans on Stop-hook blocking must be re-derived from the live doc (blocking exists, capped at 8, prompt-type default 30s), not from the pack's misread sentence.

On the human's position

Q4, verbatim: "once they actually get tot he implementation loop it's basically sit back and relax and have full confidence of when that loop is done they have shippable product… we have to close that gap", with the choice "Gates that cannot be overridden." Both halves fail the source check. Helix is not sit-back-and-relax: its fourth gate is "The engineer looks at the code and running app and decides whether the result matches their expectations", per checkpoint, and checkpoints are "the screen skeleton" then "one deliberately small section" — the human is inside the loop at high frequency, reviewing tiny diffs. Helix's confidence also comes from an oracle Joycraft lacks: behavior tests and screenshot diffs against an already-working reference app ("The reference is the spec"). A greenfield spec has no reference, so the gate collapses to tests the same agent wrote. "Cannot be overridden" is not a property any of Joycraft's hosts sells: Claude Code times out PreToolUse hooks open ("don't count on a stalled hook to act as a gate") and ends the turn after 8 consecutive Stop blocks; Codex continues the tool call on hook error; only Pi fails closed. And the repo's own history is the warning: the one blocking gate shipped as a no-op for ~2.5 months with a green test (06f08a8). My lens moves Q4 from "gates that cannot be overridden" to: gates that (a) fail closed where the host allows — CI exit codes, CLI-side status transitions (joycraft-mark-done --to done gaining a validation precondition), Pi tool_call — rather than vendor hooks as the primary vehicle; (b) are themselves tested by invoking them exactly as the harness does; (c) keep Helix's per-checkpoint human approval on small increments, which is the opposite of "sit back." Q1's "formality of the loop" survives; the "full confidence when the loop is done" phrasing does not. Q5 (Jev on the hot path) inherits the same fact: a hook that fails open on timeout is advisory by construction, whatever it is called.

P4 · 4 skeptics

Gated generation earns anything over curated skills

qualify
Ruling

Gated generation earns value over curated skills only for machine-checkable artifacts (scripts, hooks, deny patterns, CI checks) accepted by a deterministic exit-code check on inputs the generating agent did not author, run identically on every harness the project uses, with the artifact staged outside every harness-loaded directory until it merges through the normal PR path. For prose SKILL.md files the proposition does not stand: the live evidence says ungated generation lands below no-skills, the eval gate that would rescue it does not exist on any Joycraft harness, and a human-accepted agent draft is by definition a curated skill, so the claimed delta over curated is undefined.

The claim as argued

The hub may propose project-specific skills, hooks, and scripts into a separate namespace with provenance, inactive until an eval or a human accepts them, and this earns real value over shipping curated skills. Skeptic angles: SkillsBench found self-generated skills give no benefit on average; SkillOpt's gains needed a held-out score a solo dev does not have; who writes the held-out tasks; ToxicSkills and the misevolution paper; omp ships this off by default and calls it experimental.

Replacement claim

Not applicable (ruling is qualify, not flip). For reference, the claim as it survives: agent-proposed deterministic artifacts, accepted by an exit-code check the agent did not write and merged through ordinary code review, earn small real value; agent-proposed prose skills accepted by a human are curated skills and earn nothing over them.

Condition

P4 holds only when all of the following are true: (a) the generated artifact is machine-checkable -- a script, hook, deny pattern, or CI check -- never a prose SKILL.md; (b) acceptance is a deterministic exit-code check on a fixture or held-out input the generating agent did not author, strictly better than current, and the same check runs on every harness the project uses (a `command`-style grader or check.mjs exit code, not `claude plugin eval` alone); (c) the artifact is staged outside every harness-loaded directory (no .claude/skills, .agents/skills, or settings.json hooks) as a proposal plus its test until it merges through the normal PR path, and once accepted lands in a harness-neutral location or both skill dirs so a team converges rather than forks; (d) before any new namespace or ownership kind is built, the existing harden loop gets a fired-or-not measurement so the claim is tested on the one instance Joycraft already ships. On Claude Code only, a `claude plugin eval`-style with/without delta with pinned models, at least five runs per arm, and cases written by someone other than the generating agent is an acceptable additional gate. Under any weaker gate -- a human reading a diff, a Jev judgment, or the current string graders -- a generated prose skill is a curated skill with the review load relocated, and no value over curation may be claimed.

Judge's reasoning

The proposition's value lives entirely in the gate, and the panel established that neither gate variant exists in the setting Joycraft ships to. (1) Eval gate: the one study where generated beat curated (SkillOpt, all 52 cells) required a deterministic native evaluator, a 2:1:7 train/selection/test split from the same task pool (>=35 training tasks), four epochs of batch-40 rollouts, and strict-improvement acceptance. Joycraft's check.sh has five graders (output_contains/not_contains/matches, file_exists, command), no baseline arm, cannot see which skill ran, and per its README "Joycraft ships it and never runs it." `claude plugin eval` is Claude-only, defaults to 3 runs per arm, and has Claude propose the cases via `init` -- the generator authoring its own held-out set at an N inside same-model scaffold noise (0-8pp, pack section 4.5). Codex, Pi, omp, and Copilot have nothing. (2) Human gate: a person reading an agent-drafted SKILL.md and committing it is what Anthropic's skill-creator already is -- a curated skill with AI assistance. The "over curated" delta cannot be measured against itself. (3) Without a gate the baseline is not null but negative: I verified SkillsBench v4 (2026-06-14) myself -- skill-creator-generated skills score -8.1 (Claude Code + Opus 4.7), -11.3 (Codex + GPT-5.5), -11.5 (Gemini CLI) below no-skills while curated add +18.2/+19.7/+24.8 on the same configs; causes are "generated packs the solver never discovers, creator-side authoring that displaces solver work, and confidently wrong pack content." Two of those three are invisible to a visual reviewer, and the maintainer is the N=1 evaluator who "knows all the magic words" (level5 brief line 17), so the dominant failure mode is unobservable to the only person gating. (4) Joycraft already runs the exact propose-diff-approve-provenance loop in harden (Steps 3-5) and after two months the repo shows one stamped rule (AGENTS.md:36), stock deny-patterns.txt, and no outcome entry in shipped.md or decision-log.md; telemetry counts reads and skill invocations only, never whether a pattern fired. Gated generation is not new here; it is unmeasured. (5) "Inactive" is not free on the host: any SKILL.md in a loaded dir enters the 1% always-listed budget and re-attaches after compaction (pack 2.2-2.3, #64606), so inactive must mean outside every skills dir, which is a proposal document -- the intent inbox already exists for that. A generated settings.json hook is live the moment it is written and fails wrong in both directions (exit 2 blocks, timeout passes). (6) The residue that survives is real but small: executable artifacts gated by a test exit code satisfy SkillOpt's applicability clause ("executable checks"), the `command` grader in check.sh can already express it, files outside the manifest's three kinds are never touched by update, and omp proves the namespace-plus-precedence mechanism is buildable. That residue is ordinary code review of agent-written code committed through git, not a new Joycraft ownership class, and the ruling names it as the condition rather than flipping to a full refutation because every skeptic conceded it and Joycraft's ~14 already-dynamic pieces (deny patterns, folder map, build commands) are exactly this class.

Strongest refutation considered

The AI-researcher's: the only measured win for generated-over-curated (SkillOpt) came from a machine-scored held-out split Joycraft cannot supply; without it the live baseline is -8 to -11.5pp below no-skills, so the gate must recover more than 25pp just to reach curated parity; Joycraft's shippable gate cannot resolve that, `claude plugin eval` has the generator write its own cases at N=3, so "eval or human accepts" collapses to the human arm, and an agent-drafted, human-committed, provenance-stamped skill is by every study's definition a curated skill -- the delta is unmeasurable by construction, and the one gated loop already shipped (harden) has produced one stamped rule and no recorded effect in two months. I accept this refutation in full for prose skills. I did not flip outright because the same skeptic and the other three all conceded that executable artifacts under an exit-code gate are a different case (SkillOpt's own applicability clause), and because the strongest counter-evidence (SkillOpt beating human skills in all 52 cells, positive cross-model and cross-harness transfer) shows the pattern is real when the verifier is real -- which is a condition, not a refutation.

Human position moved?

Yes, on the generated half of Q1. The maintainer chose 'Gates + lifecycle + artifacts fixed; process prose generated' and named as the biggest wins the STE directive, 'the formality of the loop', and 'getting people used to TDD agentic development'. All four skeptics moved this and I concur: the panel inverts it to process prose curated and pushed once per release, deterministic checks generated behind an exit-code gate. Evidence: (1) the live SkillsBench v4 (verified) shows self-generated prose skills from Anthropic's own skill-creator landing 8-11.5pp below no skills at all, with two of the three named causes invisible to a visual reviewer; (2) the three wins the maintainer names are encoded-preference artifacts that Anthropic says persist 'only as valuable as their fidelity to your actual workflow' -- they encode Max's method, not the model's capability, and are not project-specific; (3) Q3's own wish, 'all I have to do is push the new prompting guide to an update and everyone gets the new juice', is centralized curation to fifteen colleagues, the opposite of fifteen projects each generating their own prose with no shared measurement; (4) Q4's slop gap ('hours... not shippable') is a verifier failure -- every study where generation helped, the help came from the verifier -- so the fix the maintainer wants ('gates that cannot be overridden') is P3, and adding a second unmeasured generator to a loop already producing unshippable output cuts the wrong way; (5) Q2's 'if I can get it to work best for me' makes the N=1 evaluator the person the repo's own level5 brief says cannot observe the dominant failure mode. The fixed half (gates, lifecycle, artifacts, STE) stands untouched. What survives of the generated half is the residue the ruling names: agent-proposed deterministic artifacts (deny patterns, hooks, scripts, CI checks) accepted through git with an exit-code test -- which is what harden already does and what needs measuring before anything new is built.

  • Self-generated skills (Anthropic skill-creator) score -8.1pp (Claude Code + Opus 4.7), -11.3pp (Codex + GPT-5.5), -11.5pp (Gemini CLI + Gemini 3.1 Pro) below the no-skills baseline; curated add +18.2/+19.7/+24.8pp on the same configurations; deficit attributed to 'generated packs the solver never discovers, creator-side authoring that displaces solver work, and confidently wrong pack content'; 13 of 87 tasks negative; SE +11.6pp. https://arxiv.org/html/2602.12670 (SkillsBench v4, 14 Jun 2026) -- verified by the judge via WebFetch 2026-09-24

Skeptic disagreements

  • Which artifact class may be generated: harness-expert, team-lead, and evidence-auditor restrict generation to deterministic artifacts (scripts, hooks, deny patterns, CI checks) and exclude prose SKILL.md outright; the AI-researcher does not restrict the class and instead requires a measured with/without delta on colleague-authored prompts (>=5 runs per arm) for anything generated. Ruling adopts the class restriction and accepts the AI-researcher's measured-delta gate as an additional route on Claude Code only.
  • What counts as the gate: AI-researcher -- measured delta vs no-artifact baseline on held-out prompts not authored by the generator; harness-expert -- git PR review is the gate plus a `claude plugin eval` delta with pinned models on Claude Code, proposition not claimed on other harnesses; team-lead -- a fixture or exit-code test that runs identically on every harness, explicitly not `claude plugin eval` alone because it leaves Codex developers ungated; evidence-auditor -- a deterministic executable check on tasks the agent never saw, strictly-better acceptance. Ruling takes the team-lead/evidence-auditor form (identical exit-code check on every harness) as the base condition.
  • Whether human acceptance counts as a gate at all: AI-researcher and evidence-auditor say human acceptance makes the artifact a curated skill by definition, so the delta is undefined; team-lead says it is curation relocated from the maintainer's release to the team lead's PR queue (worse, not neutral); harness-expert says git review is the right gate for executable artifacts and the resulting value is real but small and not a Joycraft feature. Ruling: human acceptance is the gate for executable artifacts via PR; for prose it converts the artifact to curated and voids the claim.
  • Whether new Joycraft machinery is warranted: harness-expert says none -- files outside the manifest kinds are already preserved, the intent inbox already stages proposals, and the value is ordinary code review; AI-researcher says ship namespace/provenance/probation mechanics if wanted but claim nothing over curation; team-lead requires committing accepted artifacts into both skill dirs or a harness-neutral scripts dir; evidence-auditor requires a manifest ownership kind and a non-joycraft- name. Ruling: measure the existing harden loop before adding any ownership class.
  • Where omp labels autolearn experimental: AI-researcher marks the pack citation misread (word absent from learn.md and manage_skill.md, 'unverified' whether it exists anywhere); harness-expert found it in packages/coding-agent/src/autolearn/settings.ts lines 7 and 17; evidence-auditor found it in docs/settings.md and the title of issue #2541; team-lead says not in tool docs, 'minor'. Resolved: the label exists in code and settings docs, so the pack's claim holds but its attribution to learn.md is imprecise; the 'NEVER edit user-authored skills' phrase is a paraphrase of authored-name shadowing.
  • SkillsBench version: AI-researcher, harness-expert, and evidence-auditor cite the live version as v4 (2026-06-14); team-lead calls it v2. I fetched it: v4. The team-lead's numbers are correct, the version label is wrong.
  • check.sh grader count: AI-researcher lists five graders including `command` (check.sh:51-64); team-lead and evidence-auditor list four (lines 52-58) and omit `command`. Verified: five, and `command` is an exit-code grader -- the very deterministic verifier the qualifiers demand, so the runner is slightly more capable than two skeptics say, though it still has no baseline arm and cannot see which skill ran.
  • Whether SkillsBench's software-engineering delta is verified: evidence-auditor and AI-researcher report v4 SE +11.6pp; team-lead could not locate the SE figure in the live text and marks it unverified. My fetch returned SE +11.6pp, resolving it.
  • Whether harden's mechanism has 'survived in production' (harness-expert, evidence-against) versus 'produced one stamped rule and no recorded effect' (AI-researcher): not contradictory -- the code shipped and runs, but nothing measures whether a hardened pattern ever blocked a command. Ruling treats it as unmeasured, not as proven.
  • Scope of the misevolution paper's lesson: all four agree the pack's 'argues for a human review gate and provenance' is the pack's inference, not the paper's (it tests SafeEvolve: critic/deleter, attribution, retirement); AI-researcher adds that SkillOpt itself is one of the 21 unsafe configurations, which none of the other three note and which cuts against relying on SkillOpt as the model of a safe gate.

Citation problems

  • Pack section 4.1 quotes SkillsBench v1 (2026-02-13): '+16.2pp across 86 tasks / 7,308 trajectories; self-generated skills provide no benefit on average; hurt 16 of 84; SE +4.5pp'. Live v4 (14 Jun 2026, verified by the judge): +16.6pp across 87 tasks, 18 configurations x 3 trials; 13 of 87 negative; SE +11.6pp; and self-generated skills are BELOW no-skills (-8.1/-11.3/-11.5pp), authored with Anthropic's skill-creator. The pack understates both the harm of ungated generation and the SE benefit of curation.
  • Pack section 1.6 attributes 'labeled experimental' and 'must NEVER edit user-authored skills' to omp docs/tools/learn.md. Neither phrase is in learn.md or manage_skill.md; 'experimental' is in packages/coding-agent/src/autolearn/settings.ts (lines 7, 17), docs/settings.md, and issue #2541's title; the NEVER phrase paraphrases authored-name shadowing (create/update returns isError with shadowed=true). Claim holds, attribution imprecise.
  • Pack section 3 inference that arXiv 2608.12851 'argues for a human review gate and provenance' is the pack's own; the paper tests SafeEvolve (automated critic/deleter, attribution, retirement), does not test human review, and lists SkillOpt among the 21 configurations that authored unsafe artifacts. Only 15 of 21 led to fresh-session harm.
  • Pack section 4.6 hardens the skill-creator post: 'capability-uplift skills become unnecessary' is 'may become less necessary... Evals tell you when'; the 'only as valuable as their fidelity to your actual workflow' clause is dropped, and it argues for curated process skills.
  • Pack section 2.9 URL code.claude.com/docs/en/plugin-eval returns 404; live page is /docs/en/plugin-evals. The pack omits that cases are proposed by Claude via `eval init`, the judge is a small fast model by default, and the feature is Claude Code only (v2.1.269+).
  • Pack section 2.10 'On Stop and SubagentStop, hooks can't block or make decisions' is contradicted by the live hooks page exit-code table: Stop exit 2 'Prevents Claude from stopping, continues the conversation.' Flagged by harness-expert; relevant to P3, not P4 -- passed to that judge.
  • Team-lead labels the live SkillsBench 'v2'; it is v4 (verified). Numbers cited are correct.
  • Team-lead and evidence-auditor state check.sh supports only four graders (lines 52-58); it has five -- `command` (exit-code grader) at check.sh:62-63. This slightly overstates the runner's poverty; the missing baseline arm and skill-identity blindness still hold.
  • Pack section 8.7 curated-harness verdict quote ('Curated, directional, in-repo context = good. Automatic, accreted = decay'): AI-researcher's grep of docs/features/2026-08-30-curated-harness/brief.md found nothing; harness-expert located it at docs/research/2026-08-30-curated-harness-brief.md:66-67. Resolved -- pack cites the wrong path.
  • AI-researcher's evidence lists check.sh at ':51-64' and harness-expert cites harden at ':56-80' while AI-researcher cites ':60-66,71-82,99-100'; all resolve to the same Steps 3-5 and Constraints text. No substantive problem.

What would change the ruling

Toward keep: a with/without delta on at least one colleague's project, with prompts written by the colleague (not the generating agent), at least five runs per arm, pinned model, showing a generated prose skill beating both the no-skill baseline and the curated Joycraft equivalent; or a SkillsBench-style study of skill-creator output passed through a human-review or lightweight-eval gate that recovers above curated parity; or `claude plugin eval` cases authored by a non-maintainer that clear the 0-8pp scaffold-noise band. Toward flip (full refutation, including the executable residue): telemetry on hardened deny patterns and generated hooks showing zero fires across the ~15 daily-driver installs after a measurement window, or a measured negative effect (blocked legitimate work, timeout pass-through) from generated hooks. Either way the precondition is the same instrument Joycraft lacks today: a fired-or-not surface for hardened patterns and a baseline-arm eval that runs on Codex and Pi as well as Claude Code.

Skeptics

AI researcherqualified
Strongest refutation

The only measured win for generated skills over curated ones (SkillOpt, all 52 cells) came from a gate Joycraft cannot supply: a machine-scored selection split carved 2:1:7 from a benchmark's own task pool (minimum 35–39 tasks), four epochs of batch-40 rollouts, 0.6M–46.4M training tokens per point of gain, and a disjoint test split for reporting. Without that gate the measured baseline is not "no benefit" but negative: SkillsBench v4 (live) has self-generated skills produced by Anthropic's own skill-creator landing 8.1pp below no-skills on Claude Code + Opus 4.7 and 11.3pp below on Codex + GPT-5.5, while curated skills add +18.2 to +24.8pp on the same configurations. So the gate must recover more than 25pp just to reach curated parity. Joycraft's shippable "eval" cannot resolve that: check.sh asserts output_contains / output_not_contains / output_matches / file_exists / command (src/templates/evals/check.sh:51-64), has no baseline arm, cannot see which skill ran, and its README says "Joycraft ships it and never runs it" (src/templates/evals/README.md:8-9). The Claude-only alternative, `claude plugin eval`, runs 3 with-arm and 3 without-arm runs per case and has Claude propose the cases ("You don't have to write the suite manually... proposes the cases and graders") — the generator authoring its own held-out set, at an N where a 0.33 Δ is inside noise (the doc itself: "One run of a non-deterministic agent tells you little"). In practice, then, the proposition's "eval or a human accepts" collapses to the human arm: a person reads a diff and commits it. An agent-drafted, human-committed, provenance-stamped skill is by every study's definition a curated skill. The "over curated" delta is therefore unmeasurable by construction in the setting Joycraft ships to, and the one gated-generation loop Joycraft already runs — harden (approve diff, stamp provenance, probation) — has produced exactly one stamped rule in two months (AGENTS.md:36) and no recorded effect (docs/context/shipped.md, decision-log.md: none).

Qualification

P4 stands only when the acceptance gate is a measured delta against a no-artifact baseline on held-out prompts not authored by the generating agent, with enough runs to separate a real effect from noise (SkillOpt's condition: dozens of tasks, multiple epochs, disjoint test split). No Joycraft project has that instrument: check.sh has no baseline arm and cannot see which skill ran; `claude plugin eval` is Claude-only, defaults to 3 runs per arm, and has Claude write the cases. Under the realistic gate — a human reading a diff — the proposition reduces to "curated skills drafted by the agent," and the claimed delta over curated is undefined. Ship the namespace, provenance, and probation mechanics if wanted (harden already proves them buildable), but do not claim value over curation, and do not turn on any generator until Joycraft ships the measurement first and shows one positive Δ on a colleague's project.

On the human's position

The maintainer's Q1 choice is "Gates + lifecycle + artifacts fixed; process prose generated," with the rationale that the biggest wins are STE, "the formality of the loop, getting people used to TDD agentic development" (pack §10, Q1). My lens attacks the second half of that choice directly. The only class of artifact the human wants generated — process prose — is the class SkillsBench measured as net-negative when self-generated (−8.1 to −11.3pp), and the thing the human names as the win (formality of the loop, TDD habit) is a fixed convention, which Anthropic's skill-creator post calls the kind that persists. The human's own Q3 answer argues against per-project generation: "all I have to do is push the new prompting guide to an update and everyone gets the new juice" is a centralized-curation model, one source pushed to fifteen colleagues, the opposite of fifteen projects each generating their own prose with no shared measurement. Q4's slop report ("some slop that took hours and that was not shippable") is the strongest evidence in the frame and it cuts against P4: the slop came from a frontier model running the current curated harness, and the proposed generator is that same model, so generation adds a second unmeasured source of variance to a loop already producing unshippable output; the fix the human wants ("gates that cannot be overridden") is P3, not P4. Q2's "if I can get it to work best for me, we can easily get it for others" is an N=1 evaluator who, per the repo's own level5 brief (line 17), "knows all the magic words" — precisely the person who cannot observe SkillsBench's dominant failure mode, generated packs the solver never discovers. Does my lens move the position? Yes, on the generated half: from "process prose generated" to "process prose deleted where the vendor says so, and anything an agent drafts is committed as a curated skill with provenance and a probation date, claiming nothing more than curated." The gates/lifecycle/STE half stands; it was never the generated part. If the maintainer wants the eval arm to be real, the precondition is a measurement Joycraft does not have: a with/without baseline, ≥5 runs per arm, on prompts a colleague wrote, before any generator ships.

Agent-harness expertqualified
Strongest refutation

P4 conflates two things and takes credit for the wrong one. (1) An agent writing a project-specific script, hook, or SKILL.md already works with zero Joycraft machinery: files outside the manifest's three kinds are never touched by update (src/install-manifest.ts:30; src/update-plan.ts:36-46 has no kind for them), Claude Code loads .claude/skills edits live (pack §2.4), Pi/omp reload on command. Whatever that earns comes from the model and the host, not Joycraft. (2) The part Joycraft would build — namespace, ownership kind, provenance, "inactive until an eval or a human accepts" — is where the claimed value has to live, and every gate variant is empty for the stated customer. Human gate: the acceptor reads a generated SKILL.md, which is exactly the scarce resource the repo's own verdicts protect (reading-fatigue: decide, don't read; curated-harness brief line 66-67: "Automatic, accreted, point-in-time state = decay"). SkillsBench v4 (live, 2026-06-14) shows the authoring model itself cannot tell: self-generated skills land BELOW the no-skills baseline on all three harnesses (−8.1 Claude Code, −11.3 Codex, −11.5 Gemini CLI), attributed to "confidently wrong pack content" and packs "the solver never discovers" — a skim-accept by a human with less context than the author is the same result with a signature on it. Joycraft has already run this exact propose→diff→approve→provenance loop for months in harden (src/skills/joycraft-harden.md Steps 3-5) and has no telemetry that one hardened pattern ever fired (src/telemetry.ts counts reads and skill invocations only) — gated generation is not a new idea here; it is an unmeasured one. Eval gate: `claude plugin eval` is Claude-only, 3 runs per case, cases written by the author or proposed by `eval init` (the generator grades its own homework), small judge model by default, and the doc itself says one run "tells you little"; a solo dev's 3-5 cases × 3 runs cannot clear the 0-8pp same-model scaffold noise (pack §4.5), while SkillOpt's strict-improvement rule needed a held-out validation set across 52 settings (live abstract). Codex/Pi/omp/Copilot have no eval hook at all, so on four of five harnesses the intent names, "eval accepts" degenerates to "human accepts". Harness cost of "inactive": a SKILL.md in a loaded skills dir is never inactive — its description enters the always-loaded 1%-budget listing and re-attaches after compaction (≤5k each, 25k combined, pack §2.2-2.3, #64606 degradation); so "inactive" must mean outside every skills dir, which is a proposal document, i.e. a spec — already the intent inbox. A generated hook in settings.json is live the moment it is written; exit 2 blocks every tool call if it is buggy and a timeout silently passes (live hooks doc) — wrong in both directions, per-vendor. Provenance does not detect misevolution: all 21 evolved configurations authored unsafe artifacts and three malicious tasks raised carryover ASR 16.0→35.3% (live 2608.12851); the fix there controlled what updates may write and reuse, not a byline. The closest precedent the pack itself cites, omp autolearn, ships default-off, labeled "(experimental)" in code, with no eval or acceptance step at all — only authored-wins and a 64KB cap. A 33k-star self-extending harness could not find a gate worth turning on by default.

Qualification

P4 survives only under all of: (a) generated artifacts are restricted to deterministic checks — scripts, hooks, deny patterns, CI checks — never prose SKILL.md files; (b) 'inactive' means staged outside every harness-loaded directory (no .claude/skills, .agents/skills, settings.json hooks) as a proposal document plus a test, and 'accepted' means merged through the normal PR/code-review gate — git is the gate, not new Joycraft ownership machinery; (c) on Claude Code the proposal additionally carries a `claude plugin eval`-style Δ with pinned models, and on Codex/Pi/omp/Copilot the proposition is not claimed at all; (d) before building anything new, the existing harden loop gets a telemetry surface (did a hardened pattern ever fire?) so the claim 'gated generation earns something' is measured on the one instance Joycraft already ships. Under those conditions the 'value over curated skills' is real but small and is not a Joycraft feature — it is ordinary code review of agent-written code.

On the human's position

The maintainer's Q1 — "Gates + lifecycle + artifacts fixed; process prose generated" — is P4 stated at the scale of the whole harness, and my lens moves it. Process prose is the one artifact class the live evidence says generation is worst at (SkillsBench v4: self-generated packs below no-skills, 'confidently wrong'), and the class Anthropic says is durable when curated (encoded team workflow) — so the human proposes to regenerate the thing that persists and keep fixed the things that already are code. Invert it: process prose deleted (P7/P8's job), checks generated. The Q1 rationale names the real invariants — "the STE language directive, the formality of the loop, getting people used to TDD agentic development" — and none of those is project-specific; they are one curated artifact per release, which is exactly what the Q3 wish "push the new prompting guide to an update and everyone gets the new juice" describes: curated distribution, not per-project generation. Q3 argues against P4, not for it. Q4 — "recent sessions I've been getting some slop that took hours and that was not shippable, we have to close that gap" — is the strongest thing in the frame and generation does nothing for it: every study where generation helped, the help came from the verifier (SkillOpt's held-out score, Voyager's self-verification, Helix's blocking reviewers), and a generated per-project skill adds a reader load and a description-budget cost between the human and that verifier. The 'about fifteen colleagues across teams of different sizes' fact cuts the same way: per-project generated skills committed to a shared repo become accreted team state the curated-harness brief already condemned, and per-user generated skills fork behavior across a team (P11's conflict). What survives from the human's position is the residue I qualify on: harden-style deterministic artifacts (scripts, hooks, deny patterns, CI checks) proposed by the agent and accepted through git — which is already shipped and needs measurement, not a new namespace.

Team lead, five engineersqualified
Strongest refutation

For a team, the proposition's value lives entirely in the gate, and the only gate a five-person Claude+Codex team can actually run today is a human reading a generated SKILL.md in a PR. That is the curation the proposal claims to displace, moved from the maintainer's release (once, tested, shared) to the team lead's review queue (five developers, per project, per PR). The eval alternative does not exist on the team's surfaces: Joycraft's own runner has four string assertions and no skill invokes it (src/templates/evals/check.sh:52-58; only src/templates/evals/README.md references it); `claude plugin eval` is Claude-only, so the Codex half of the team gets no baseline delta; SkillOpt's gate "accepted only when it strictly improves a held-out validation score" needs per-project held-out tasks that nobody on a five-person team owns or writes. The artifact the gate would review is the one SkillsBench (live v2) says a skill-creator produces: packs "the solver never discovers" and "confidently wrong pack content", landing 8.1pp below no skills on Claude Code + Opus 4.7 and 11.3pp below on Codex + GPT-5.5. Those are the two defects a visual reviewer of mixed seniority cannot see, and ToxicSkills describes the same blind spot: skills that "appear functionally legitimate when reviewed visually" and misbehave only at runtime. Consistency is worse, not better: Claude Code reads .claude/skills, Codex reads .agents/skills only (learn.chatgpt.com/docs/build-skills, 2026-09-24), and the private profile gitignores both (src/gitignore.ts:31), so a skill generated on developer A's machine either never reaches developer B or lands as an untested prose file in a PR. Generated prose skills therefore earn nothing over a curated, committed set for a team. What Joycraft already generates well (deny patterns with provenance, folder map, build commands, stack detection; pack §8.5) is data or checks verified by code, and that is the only class where generation has earned anything here.

Qualification

Gated generation earns value over curated skills ONLY when all three hold: (1) the generated artifact is machine-checkable — a deny pattern, a script, a hook, or a check with a fixture whose pass/fail is an exit code, not a prose SKILL.md; (2) the gate runs identically on every harness the team uses (a script test or `check.mjs`-style exit code, not `claude plugin eval` alone, which leaves Codex developers ungated); (3) an accepted artifact is committed to the repo in both `.agents/skills` and `.claude/skills` (or a harness-neutral scripts dir) so five developers converge rather than fork. Generated prose skills fail (1) and, per SkillsBench v2, are expected to land below the no-skills baseline; for them, \"proposal into a PR a human reads\" is curation with the review load relocated to the team lead, and the proposition does not stand.

The generator was Anthropic's skill-creator, the same precedent the pack cites in §2.14. On the human's position

The maintainer's Q1 is \"Gates + lifecycle + artifacts fixed; process prose generated\", with the rationale that the biggest wins are \"the STE language directive, the formality of the loop, getting people used to TDD agentic development as opposed to endless vibe coding (the essence and core objective of joycraft)\". Those three wins are all shared process prose. On a five-person team, the loop's formality is only a win if all five run the same loop; generating process prose per project gives me five dialects of TDD-agentic-development and a junior who learns a dialect the senior does not recognize. The maintainer's own examples argue for curated, committed prose, not generated prose. Q2 says \"if I can get it to work best for me, we can easily get it for others... I'll make content etc.. around to teach people, but the hope also being that as this system gets... more driven by the harness this becomes a non issue.\" For a team lead it is the opposite: teaching content presupposes a stable thing to teach, and a harness that regenerates its process per project has none; \"driven by the harness\" moves the curation from his release (once, tested) into my PR queue (per developer, untested, prose). My lens moves the position from \"process prose generated\" to \"process prose curated and committed once; project-specific checks, scripts, deny patterns, and hooks generated, each with a fixture or exit-code test, promoted into both skill dirs only after that test passes.\" The 15 daily-driver colleagues he cites are the strongest fact against his own Q1.

Evidence auditorqualified
Strongest refutation

The only study that shows generated skills beating curated ones (SkillOpt, arxiv 2605.23904) earns its gain from a machine gate the proposition cannot supply: a deterministic native evaluator, a 2:1:7 train/selection/test split of the same task distribution (e.g. 140 held-out selection environments for ALFWorld), four epochs of rollout batches of 40, and acceptance only when the held-out score strictly increases. Joycraft's eval graders are output_contains / output_not_contains / output_matches / file_exists (src/templates/evals/check.sh:52-58); nothing in the repo scores a skill against a held-out task set, and no skill writes a skill today (grep of src/skills/*.md: only implement, implement-feature and optimize mention SKILL.md, all as readers). Without that gate, the live SkillsBench text says self-generated skills are not "no benefit on average" as the pack claims but net negative on every configuration tested: -8.1 pp (Claude Code + Opus 4.7), -11.3 pp (Codex + GPT-5.5), -11.5 pp (Gemini CLI + Gemini 3.1 Pro) versus a no-skills baseline, while curated skills gained +18.2 / +19.7 / +24.8 pp on the same three (arxiv.org/html/2602.12670, latest version 2026-06-14). The pack quoted the superseded v1 abstract (86 tasks, 7,308 trajectories, +16.2 pp, 16 of 84 hurt, SWE +4.5 pp); the current version reports 87 tasks, 18 configurations, +16.6 pp, 13 of 87 hurt, SWE +11.6 pp. So the pack understates both the harm of ungated generation and the benefit of curation in software engineering. The remaining half of the proposed gate, "or a human accepts", has no study behind it at all; a human reading and approving an agent-drafted SKILL.md is a curated skill authored with AI assistance, which is exactly what Anthropic's skill-creator already is. The proposition therefore does not earn value OVER curated skills; where it works it IS curated skills, and where it is automatic it needs a verifier the target users do not have.

Qualification

P4 stands only when (a) the generated artifact is scored by a deterministic executable check on tasks the generating agent never saw (a held-out selection split, as SkillOpt requires), (b) acceptance is 'strictly better than current' on that check, and (c) the artifact is a hook or script, not a process-prose skill. Under any weaker gate — 'a human accepts', a Jev judgment, or the repo's current output_contains graders — the live SkillsBench evidence predicts a net loss versus curated skills, and the proposition is refuted as stated.

On the human's position

Q1: the maintainer fixes 'gates + lifecycle + artifacts' and makes 'process prose generated', while naming as the biggest wins the STE directive, 'the formality of the loop', and 'getting people used to TDD agentic development'. Those three wins are exactly the encoded-preference kind that Anthropic's post calls durable 'only as valuable as their fidelity to your actual workflow' (claude.com/blog, 2026-03-03), and SkillsBench's live text puts unaided generation of such prose at -8 to -11.5 pp below no skills at all. My lens moves the position: process prose is the thing to keep curated, because it encodes the maintainer's method, not the model's capability; what can be generated behind a gate is executable (hooks, scripts) where a test exit code is the verifier. Q4: 'gates that cannot be overridden' — agreed as a goal, but for generated artifacts the eval half of the gate does not exist in the repo (check.sh:52-58 has four string graders and no held-out scoring), so today the gate reduces to the human, and human review of marketplace skills still passed a 13.4% critical rate (Snyk). Q2: 'me truly first as I am the super user' — the maintainer is the one user who could write held-out tasks for his own projects; that is a personal workflow, not evidence the feature earns value for the fifteen colleagues. Q5's 'insanely good and basically free' Jev does not rescue P4: SkillOpt's gate is deterministic and held-out; Jev is a literal-reading probabilistic judge that the gated agent can steer (pack section 7.8), so it cannot stand in as the acceptance verifier. Condition under which the position survives: generation is limited to artifacts that a deterministic, held-out check the agent did not write can score, with a manifest ownership kind and a non-joycraft- name; process-prose skills stay curated.

P5 · 4 skeptics

Fetch-and-subtract model profiles beat per-model docs

qualify
Ruling

P5 as written ("fetch-and-subtract beats per-model docs") does not stand: all four skeptics, from four lenses, converge on the same fault line, that the expensive and valuable part of the per-model job is selection and condensation, not delivery, and fetch changes only where the raw material comes from. The "subtract" half stands fully sourced. P5 survives only as: curated, condensed, dated per-model profiles remain the delivered artifact (today's vendor-kind `update` path); vendor guides are fetched only as an authoring aid or change detector, discovered via llms.txt with redirects followed and slugs never constructed, and never placed raw into agent context; profile installation keys to the running model rather than the harness; new or retuned blocks land only behind a measured with/without delta.

The claim as argued

Model guidance should be fetched from the vendor's predictable Markdown URL with a dated bundled fallback (Codex openai-docs precedent), and the per-model job becomes an audit that removes instructions the vendor now says to drop; the maintainer also wants "push the new prompting guide to an update and everyone gets the new juice." Skeptic angles: URL stability is unverified; Claude Code already injects the Fable block so a profile duplicates the harness; vendor pages target API developers; open-weight vendors publish nothing; Cursor says reading docs is not enough, it tunes with evals over weeks.

Replacement claim

Curated per-model profiles remain the delivered artifact; vendor guides are fetched only as an authoring or change-detection input, discovered via llms.txt with redirects followed, never slug-constructed and never placed raw into agent context; the per-model job is selection plus the optimize Step 2c subtract audit; installation keys to the running model; blocks are added or retuned only behind a measured delta.

Condition

P5 holds only if all of the following are true: (1) the delivered artifact stays a curated, condensed, dated per-model profile with stable cited headings, shipped as vendor-kind through `joycraft update`, today's mechanism; (2) 'fetch' is confined to an authoring aid or change detector, either a repo-local maintainer skill under src/local-skills/ that diffs the vendor .md against the profile and drafts a subtract list, or an update-time currency check against platform.claude.com/llms.txt and developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/latest-model.md that follows redirects, never constructs slugs for unlisted models, falls back silently offline, and never places fetched vendor text into agent context unsummarized; (3) the 'subtract' half is optimize Step 2c plus parked spec 8, run against the installed profile, advisory only; (4) profile installation is keyed to the running model read from harness config, not to the harness, so open-weight and unknown models on Pi/omp receive no Claude-shaped profile; (5) any new or retuned block lands only behind a measured with/without delta, and the first such run tests whether the profile does anything at all inside Claude Code given the partial harness injection observed. Under these conditions 'beats per-model docs' collapses to 'per-model docs with faster authoring and a currency signal'; if the shape stays runtime CLI fetch with a dated bundled fallback replacing the curated doc, the proposition is refuted.

Judge's reasoning

Three facts settle the framing. First, the maintainer's wish is already shipped: the profile is `kind: vendor`, `ownership: verified` in docs/.joycraft/manifest.json:951-955 (I read it), install-manifest.ts:30 defines three kinds with vendor replaced on every `update`, and main merges auto-release (AGENTS.md "Release behavior"; 19 publishes in nine weeks per the maintainer skeptic). So "push the guide to an update" distinguishes nothing between fetch and bundle; both are "maintainer pushes". Second, the fetched artifact is not a profile: the live Fable 5.1 page is 6,610 words / 16 H2s (four skeptics independently confirmed the count to the digit), roughly ten sections are API-only or off Joycraft's surface, and the parked Opus 5.5 brief's own table (which I read from feature/opus-5-5-prompting) scores 4 act / 2 handled by Claude Code / 5 not applicable. The pack's own §6 inference concedes "the useful step is condensing". That condensation is per-model authoring; the 9-spec decomposition shows only spec 2 writes prose, the rest wire loops, the updater, optimize and autofix, none of which fetch removes. Third, the heading contract: seven skills cite the installed profile by path and block heading, and tests/model-profile-citations.test.ts (I read lines 10-45) enforces that every cited heading exists; vendor headings differ from profile headings and across models, so a raw fetched doc breaks the contract or needs a per-model heading map, which is a per-model doc by another name. The "subtract" half is the strongest part of P5 and already ships: optimize Step 2c (src/skills/joycraft-optimize.md:72-84, I read it) flags anti-formatting and hand-holding rules as MODEL_SUPERSEDED against named profile blocks, advisory only; parked spec 8 extends it to thinking rules. Every vendor "remove X" quote the pack relies on was verified verbatim by at least one skeptic, and I verified the one they disagreed on. The Codex precedent does not support the mechanism claimed: openai-docs is a documentation-lookup skill driven by agent web search on a resolver URL with opaque returned URLs, its bundled fallback is undated and self-described non-authoritative, and Codex's actual per-model steering is bundled models.json shipped by release, the very thing P5 says to abandon. Two lens-specific findings sharpen the qualification. The solo-pi lens shows D6 keys the profile to the harness (model-profile.ts:20, "Pi and omp run Claude models") while this repo's own AGENTS.md runs Pi on kimi-k3 and the maintainer's models-store lists six open-weight models, so "everyone gets the new juice" today means a Qwen run receives Anthropic steering; Pi's system prompt never names the model, so a fetcher has no URL to pick. The ai-researcher lens shows no with/without measurement exists for the profile at all and that the vendor itself says adjacent-release prompts "should perform well without changes"; I adopt the eval requirement for new blocks (it is already in the lead's own item 5, "retune only with a measured delta") but do not adopt "delete the profile if Δ≈0" as a ruling, because on Pi running Claude the harness injects nothing, so the profile is not redundant there. URL stability is now characterized rather than unverified: the pattern is four months old, applies only to the six models that received a guide (sibling guesses 404, including my own guess in this session), the hostname moved twice with redirects preserved, one slug was renamed with a 308, and pages carry no version, ETag or Last-Modified; so a fetcher is viable only if it discovers via llms.txt and follows redirects, and it cannot cheaply detect change.

Strongest refutation considered

The maintainer skeptic's: fetch does not remove the expensive part of the per-model job (human selection of which vendor sections apply to a repo-bound CLI harness, plus keeping ten stable headings for seven citing skills) and adds a mechanism the maintainer owns forever (network module with deadline/cache/backoff/redirects, offline policy, fetch stubs in every touching test after the 2026-06-11 unmocked-fetch breakage, a new ownership kind or cache path for the dated fallback, 54 KB per check with no conditional GET), while the distribution it promises already exists as vendor-kind replacement on `update` with automatic releases faster than Anthropic's guide cadence. I found no skeptic evidence that rebuts this, and the evidence-auditor's cadence facts (Fable profile shipped 22 days after the guide; Opus 5.5 decomposed within two days; "months behind" is Aider's number) confirm the currency problem fetch would solve is not measured in this repo.

Human position moved?

Yes, on the mechanism; not on the park. The maintainer's Q3 wish, "all I have to do is push the new prompting guide to an update and everyone gets the new juice," is already the shipped behavior: the profile is kind: vendor in docs/.joycraft/manifest.json:951-955, `update` replaces it with a backup, and main merges auto-release; PR #78 delivered the Fable profile exactly that way, 22 days after the guide. All four skeptics landed on this independently and I confirmed the manifest row. So the panel moves the position from 'build fetch so the update carries the guide' to 'the update already carries it; the hours go to selecting which vendor sections apply and keeping the ten cited headings stable, and no fetch shortens that.' Three further moves with evidence: 'everyone' is wrong for the maintainer's own fleet, since model-profile.ts:20 keys the profile to the harness and AGENTS.md runs Pi on kimi-k3 and Codex on GPT-6, so two of three harnesses either get Claude steering wrongly or nothing; 'juice' is unmeasured, since no with/without run exists and the vendor's own pages say adjacent-release prompts perform well unchanged; and hand condensation already dropped a sentence the vendor calls load-bearing ('The user is not watching in real time', absent from profile:39-43), which argues for verbatim dated vendor blocks behind a measurement, not for automating the same ungated condensation. The park itself is defensible on hours, but the stated reason, 'it may become moot', is not supported: nothing in a fetch design removes the work the nine parked specs do (Applies-to tags, row swap, unattended instruction in Pi loop and autofix, optimize extension), and parked spec 8 is the subtract half of P5 already written. Where the maintainer is right against the panel: a hand-written doc per model at a ~3-week guide cadence is a recurring feature, and the profile is already drifting from a vendor mirror into Joycraft house style (End State of Every Prompt, Paths to Choose Between), which is exactly the curated value a fetch cannot produce.
