  • Claude Code harness duplication (pack §6.5): maintainer and ai-researcher report first-hand that the subagent system prompt does not contain the 'You are operating autonomously' block; ai-researcher and solo-pi report the batching instruction is present verbatim and the guide's 'first privately list' nudge is appended to tool results (the judge observed both in this session too); evidence-auditor has only a gist search snippet as corroboration. Solo-pi notes duplication is Claude Code only, Pi injects neither.
  • Whether the D6 harness-keying is a defect P5 must fix: solo-pi and ai-researcher both attack it (kimi-k3 on Pi receives Fable steering); maintainer and evidence-auditor do not raise it.
  • Whether hand condensation already introduced an error: ai-researcher finds the profile's fenced autonomy block (profile:39-43) omits 'The user is not watching in real time', a sentence the guide says 'carries much of the effect. Keep it as written.' The judge confirmed the sentence is absent from the profile but did not fetch the guide lines 809/815; no other skeptic checked.
  • Cost of the fetch mechanism: maintainer estimates ~300 lines plus tests and a settings policy; ai-researcher and solo-pi say the cost is low because update-check.ts already has cache, 3s deadline and backoff to reuse.

Citation problems

  • §6.3 'Codex's openai-docs skill ... only as a disclosed fallback' as a precedent for dated-bundled-fallback fetch: quote holds but is misapplied. The skill is a documentation-lookup assistant using agent web search on a resolver URL, returned URLs treated as opaque (no slug derivation), fallback undated and self-described 'non-authoritative'. Codex's real per-model steering is bundled models.json. Open issue #43164 (2026-09-06) shows fetch-first breaking offline instructions.
  • §6.2 'Open-weight vendors: none found': factually wrong. Moonshot publishes prompt-best-practice.md, kimi-k3-quickstart.md and a tool-calling page indexed in platform.kimi.ai/docs/llms.txt; Qwen model cards carry a Best Practices section. The conclusion survives because the content is sampling and reasoning_effort guidance with no subtractive steering.
  • §6.4 Opus 5.5 migration quote 'Instructions tuned for Claude Opus 5's behavior may no longer be needed': the ai-researcher's 'misread' verdict is itself wrong; judge verified the quote verbatim at platform.claude.com/docs/en/models/opus-5-5/migration-guide.md line 1160 (200, 9,399 words as the pack states).
  • §6.4 'CRITICAL: You MUST' overtriggers on 4.5/4.6: exact phrase not found by grep in claude-prompting-best-practices.md; the overtrigger guidance exists in other words at lines 489 and 528.
  • §6.4 OpenAI 'Guidance that helps Sol or Luna may overconstrain GPT-6 Astra': not found on developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/latest-model.md by two skeptics; unverified. The 'more sensitive to instructions contained in skills' sentence does hold there.
  • §6.5 Claude Code injects the Fable 5.1 'You are operating autonomously...' block verbatim: unverified for the main agent and contradicted for subagents by three first-hand observations (maintainer, ai-researcher, judge). What is confirmed is partial injection: the batching instruction verbatim in the system prompt and the guide's 'first privately list' nudge appended to tool results.
  • §6 Contradicting 'Cursor's weeks of eval-driven tuning says reading docs is not enough': the 'weeks' and literal/tolerant sentences are verbatim at cursor.com/blog/continually-improving-agent-harness (2026-04-30); 'reading docs is not enough' is the pack's inference, Cursor does not say it. The ai-researcher could not locate the source at all.
  • §6 Inference 'Static tables fall months behind': that is Aider's figure (357 entries, ~5 months). Joycraft's Fable profile shipped 21-22 days after the guide and the Opus 5.5 feature was decomposed within two days of release.
  • §2.15 'URL-slug stability UNVERIFIED': now characterizable. The pattern is four months old, holds only for the six models listed in llms.txt (sibling and judge-guessed slugs 404), the hostname moved twice with redirects, one slug was renamed with a 308, and pages carry no version, ETag or Last-Modified (cache-control: private, no-store). Stability is conditional on llms.txt discovery and redirect following, and change detection needs a full-text diff.
  • §6.3 'dated bundled fallback' wording in the candidate shape: neither Codex precedent (openai-docs references, models.json) carries a date stamp as the pack implies; the 'dated' property would be Joycraft's invention, not a borrowed pattern.

What would change the ruling

Toward flip in P5's favor (fetch beats curated docs): a measured eval in which raw or lightly trimmed vendor guide text in agent context outperforms the condensed profile on Joycraft's own tasks; plus a vendor stability contract for the guide pages (version or date in frontmatter, ETag or Last-Modified, or a resolver like OpenAI's latest-model.md that Anthropic does not offer today); plus a harness-side model-identity signal on Pi and omp so the fetcher knows which URL applies. Toward flip against any profile (drop per-model prose entirely): a with/without run inside Claude Code (claude plugin eval against a no-profile baseline, or a ce-retune-style A/B with a registered noise floor) showing the profile's delta is ~0 or negative, together with confirmation that the main-agent system prompt already carries the full autonomy block. Toward keep as written: evidence that maintainer condensation hours dominate release cost (wall-clock, not spec counts) and that vendor pages change materially between releases at a rate that a 3-week release cadence misses; nothing in the pack or any skeptic return measures either.

Skeptics

Maintainer counting hoursqualified
Strongest refutation

Fetch does not remove the expensive part of the per-model job and adds a mechanism I must own forever. The expensive part is curation, not distribution: the Fable profile is 1,267 words with 10 stable headings that 7 skills cite by name and two test files enforce (tests/model-profile-citations.test.ts:16-40, tests/model-profile-template.test.ts); the live vendor page is 6,610 words with 16 headings whose text differs from the profile's ("Finish the whole task" vs "Finish the Whole Task"; "Writing density" vs "Mannered Prose") and differs again per model (Opus 5.5 says "Unattended agentic runs" for the same concept). A fetched doc either breaks the heading contract or needs a per-model heading map, which is a per-model doc by another name. The Opus 5.5 brief shows where the hours actually go: 9 specs, of which only spec 2 is "write the blocks"; the human judgment that 5 of 11 vendor sections do not apply to a CLI harness (max_tokens, thinking-disabled, multi-app, vision, frontend) is the work, and a raw fetch hands the agent all eleven. Distribution is already solved: the profile is `kind: vendor` in the manifest (docs/.joycraft/manifest.json:951-955), so every `update` replaces it, and releases are automatic on main merge (19 npm publishes 2026-07-21 → 2026-09-24, ~3x faster than Anthropic's ~3-week guide cadence). Meanwhile fetch costs: a network module with deadline/cache/backoff (the update-check.ts:97-400 shape, ~300 lines), a settings policy for offline/private machines, fetch stubs in every test that touches it (the 2026-06-11 suite breakage was exactly an unmocked fetch), redirect handling (the vendor domain moved twice and one slug was renamed: docs.anthropic.com → docs.claude.com → platform.claude.com, claude-4-best-practices → claude-prompting-best-practices, 308 observed 2026-09-24), no conditional GET (`cache-control: private, no-store`, no ETag, 54 KB per check), and a fourth ownership kind or a new cache path for the dated fallback. The "subtract" half already ships as optimize Step 2c (src/skills/joycraft-optimize.md:72-80) against the curated doc. The Codex precedent is misread: its skill tells the agent to web-search official domains and its fallback is a vendor-authored reference file, not a dated snapshot of a fetched URL; OpenAI copying OpenAI's own docs costs OpenAI nothing, while Joycraft copying Anthropic's is the per-model job again.

Qualification

Survives only if "fetch" runs on the maintainer's machine at authoring time, as a repo-local skill under src/local-skills/ (never bundled), that diffs the vendor .md against the curated profile and drafts a subtract list. The CLI never fetches; the curated per-model profile stays the installed, cited home; no new ownership kind, cache path, or settings policy; optimize Step 2c stays the user-side audit. Under that condition the per-model doc is kept and only its authoring gets faster. If the shape stays runtime fetch in the CLI with a dated bundled fallback, my verdict is refuted.

On the human's position

The maintainer wrote (Q3): "I'm thinking that basically we can help this in the new system where all I have to do is push the new prompting guide to an update and everyone gets the new juice." From my lens this is already true and has been since 0.7.16: the profile is `kind: vendor` (manifest.json:951-955), an `update` replaces it, and main merges publish automatically (19 releases in nine weeks). Nothing in the fetch proposal shortens that path; the thing that costs hours is deciding which of eleven vendor sections apply to a repo-bound CLI harness and keeping the ten headings stable for the seven skills that cite them. The parked Opus 5.5 brief is the receipt: 9 specs, one of them writing prose. So my lens moves the position from "build fetch so the update carries the guide" to "the update already carries it; spend the hours on a maintainer-side authoring aid and keep the curated doc." His Q3 choice to park is right for the wrong reason: it is not moot under fetch, it is the same curation job with a network module bolted on. Where he is right against me: a hand-written doc per model at Anthropic's ~3-week cadence is a recurring feature, and the two Fable-era operator blocks ("End State of Every Prompt", "Paths to Choose Between") already show the doc drifting from a vendor mirror into Joycraft house style, which no fetch could produce and no audit would flag.

AI researcherqualified
Strongest refutation

P5 compares two delivery mechanisms for a document whose effect has never been measured. Nothing in the pack or the repo measures the Joycraft profile with vs without on any task; the only quantitative claims are the vendor's internal evals, and the vendor's own pages say the opposite of "fetch and apply": "Your existing Claude Fable 5 prompts should perform well on Claude Fable 5.1 without changes" (Fable 5.1 guide, line 9), "Existing Claude Opus 5 prompts should perform well without changes" (Opus 5.5 guide, para 2), and every block carries "check that trade-off on your own tasks" / "test several levels against your own evals rather than carrying over" / "measure the effect on your own tasks". The vendor treats its blocks as hypotheses for your eval, not a spec to transplant. The literature agrees: the harness ablation (arXiv 2609.20804, 2026-09-17) puts explicit process instruction at -2.0 to -0.4% on the strongest models; Gloaguen et al. (2602.11988) find context files "do not generally improve task success" and add >20% cost; Harness-Bench (2605.27922) shows a 23.8pp spread across harnesses for the same backend, so a block tested in Anthropic's Messages-API harness does not automatically transfer into Claude Code, which already injects overlapping text (this session's system prompt carries the batching instruction verbatim as in profile lines 134-135, and the Fable guide's batching nudge was appended to a tool result mid-session). The "fetch" half is further broken on mechanics: the Fable 5.1 .md is 898 lines of which 685 (76%) are API code samples for turn-scoped system messages and beta headers, so fetching delivers mostly irrelevant content and forces a condensation step, which is exactly the ungated rewrite ACE (2510.04618) shows collapsing a playbook below the no-adaptation baseline; the Anthropic .md is served cache-control: private, no-store with no ETag or Last-Modified, so "the vendor now says drop X" requires a full-text diff against a snapshot, not a cheap freshness check; and on Pi/omp the running model is not named in the system prompt (parked brief, Hard Constraints), while this repo's own AGENTS.md:182 runs Pi on kimi-k3 and :181 runs Codex on GPT-6, so the fetcher has no URL to choose and D6 already ships Fable steering to a Pi harness running an open-weight model. The Codex precedent is misapplied: openai-docs is a docs-lookup skill answered on demand, its bundled references are undated, and issue #43164 (opened 2026-09-06, open) shows fetch-first ignoring offline instructions.

Qualification

P5 survives only in this form: (1) the bundled artifact is a dated, verbatim snapshot of the vendor's block text per model, shipped through `update` as `vendor` kind — which is a per-model doc, so 'beats per-model docs' collapses to 'per-model docs without hand condensation'; (2) the per-model job is the subtract audit that optimize Step 2c already runs, checking skills and AGENTS.md against that snapshot; (3) no block is added, kept, or retuned without a measured with/without delta (claude plugin eval Δ against a no-profile baseline, or a ce-retune-style A/B with a registered noise floor), and the first such run must test whether the profile does anything at all inside Claude Code given the harness already injects overlapping text; (4) live fetch is dropped for Pi, omp, Codex and any open-weight model, because the running model is unknown or no vendor page exists, and is at most an optional freshness check for Claude Code after (3) shows a positive delta. Absent (3), the proposition is unfalsifiable and should not drive a spec.

On the human's position

The maintainer's words (Q3, park): "all I have to do is push the new prompting guide to an update and everyone gets the new juice." Three attacks. First, "juice" is asserted, not measured: the vendor's own pages say Fable 5 and Opus 5 prompts "should perform well without changes" on their successors, and the strongest-model ablation (2609.20804) puts process prose at -2.0 to -0.4%. The profile shipped in PR #78 without a with/without run, and `claude plugin eval` (v2.1.269, 3 runs against a no-plugin baseline) has existed since 2026-09-11 to get that number. Second, "push to an update" already works: the profile is `vendor` kind (install-manifest.ts:30), PR #78 delivered it through `update`, and the parked feature's spec 3 swaps the row. The bottleneck is the maintainer's hours condensing a 6,610-word page by hand, not a delivery mechanism, and fetch only buys between-release freshness that the vendor says is low-value. Third, "everyone" is wrong for his own fleet: AGENTS.md:181-182 runs Codex on GPT-6 and Pi on kimi-k3, so two of his three harnesses have no Claude juice to receive, and D6 (model-profile.ts:20) already ships Fable steering to Pi regardless of the model it runs. One point supports his instinct against hand-written docs: the hand condensation dropped 'The user is not watching in real time' (profile:40-42), the sentence the guide says 'carries much of the effect. Keep it as written.' Hand editing introduced an error the vendor warned about. But the fix is verbatim vendor blocks behind a measurement, not a fetch pipeline that automates the same ungated condensation. Does my lens move his position? Yes, from 'park until the new system pushes guides' to 'park until a with/without Δ exists'. If the eval Δ is ~0, delete the profile and keep only the subtract audit in optimize Step 2c; if it is positive, ship verbatim dated vendor snapshots through `update` and skip live fetch entirely.

Solo dev on Pi, open-weight modelqualified
Strongest refutation

P5 conflates delivery with content. The thing that helps a coding agent is the condensed, model-tagged profile (1,267 words, docs/templates/reference/model-profile-claude-fable-5-1.md), not the vendor page: the live Fable 5.1 Markdown is 6,610 words and most of its body is API-integration material (append-only history, prefix_mismatch_behavior, prompt-cache, thinking blocks, effort parameter; fetched 2026-09-24). Someone still has to decide which sections apply, which the parked Opus 5.5 brief did by hand (4 of 11 sections "Act", 5 "Not applicable"). That decision IS a per-model doc; fetching only changes where its raw material comes from. For my model the mechanism has nothing to fetch and nothing to subtract: Qwen model cards and Moonshot's docs publish sampling and reasoning_effort guidance, not behavioral steering or "remove this for older models" language (huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-235B-A22B README; platform.kimi.ai/docs/guide/prompt-best-practice.md; kimi-k3-quickstart.md, all fetched 2026-09-24). Worse, Joycraft already ships me the wrong vendor's profile: src/model-profile.ts:19-20 installs the Fable doc for 'pi' and 'omp' on the fable-native D6 rationale "Pi and omp users run Claude models" (docs/features/2026-09-22-fable-native-sdlc-harness/brief.md:33-37), while this machine's ~/.pi/agent/models-store.json lists kimi-k3, qwen3p8-max, deepseek-v4-pro and glm-5p3 under moonshotai, deepseek and fireworks providers. Pi 0.80.10's dist/core/system-prompt.js (109 lines) never references the model, so the parked brief's fallback rule "apply every block tagged for any current Claude model" would apply Anthropic's steering to a Qwen run. Fetch-and-subtract keyed to a Claude URL makes that worse, not better. Finally the "Codex precedent" is misread in shape: Codex hits one stable resolver URL, treats returned guide URLs "as opaque: fetch those exact URLs without deriving, substituting, or appending", and its bundled latest-model.md calls itself "a compact, non-authoritative fallback" with no date (codex-rs/skills/src/assets/samples/openai-docs/references/model-migration.md:30, latest-model.md:3, fetched 2026-09-24). Anthropic offers no resolver, only llms.txt; its docs moved docs.anthropic.com -> docs.claude.com -> platform.claude.com and renamed claude-4-best-practices to claude-prompting-best-practices (all redirect to 200 today; prompting-claude-opus-4-6.md is 404). Stability is "redirects have held so far", not a contract.

P5 survives only as: (1) fetch at `update` time (already online for npm; src/update-check.ts:97,328 is the existing fetch-with-cache-and-3s-deadline pattern), never at session start, where a 6,610-word page would cost a per-token API user roughly 5x the tokens of the condensed profile every session; (2) the fetched page is raw material for a condensation pass whose output stays a short profile with `Applies to:` tags per block (the parked D1 shape), and that condensed doc, dated, is what installs and what the bundled fallback is; (3) the profile install is keyed to the actual running model read from the harness config (Pi models.json / session model, Claude Code's system prompt), not to the harness as src/model-profile.ts:20 does today; open-weight and unknown models get no vendor profile, or an explicit "no vendor guidance; keep scaffolding" stub, never Claude's; (4) Anthropic discovery goes through platform.claude.com/llms.txt with redirects followed, OpenAI through the latest-model resolver, and both fall back to the dated bundle when the fetch fails or the slug 404s; (5) the subtract step stays the existing optimize Step 2c audit (src/skills/joycraft-optimize.md:74-84, RETIRE/PROBATION, advisory) and tune's `probation:` model comment, which need a profile with stable headings, not a fetch.

On the human's position

Q3, verbatim: \"all I have to do is push the new prompting guide to an update and everyone gets the new juice.\" That push already exists and needs no fetch: the profile is a vendor-owned template (src/model-profile.ts:14; ownership kind vendor in src/install-manifest.ts), so bumping the template and releasing makes the next `update` replace it, backing up edited copies under docs/.joycraft/local/replaced/. What the sentence hides is the word \"everyone\". On my lens \"everyone gets the new juice\" means a Pi user on Kimi K3 or Qwen 3.8 gets Anthropic's Fable steering, because D6 keyed the install to the harness on the false premise that Pi users run Claude models (brief.md:33-37) and Pi cannot tell the skill what model is running. The push mechanism is fine; the content must be keyed to the model actually running, and for my model the honest content is \"no vendor guidance exists; keep the scaffolding\", which the inverted-U result supports. My lens moves the position from \"push the guide\" to \"push a condensed, dated, model-tagged profile, installed only where the running model matches, with nothing Claude-shaped landing on open-weight runs.\" On the Park decision itself: the parked D1 (one Claude doc, Applies-to tags) and spec 5 (Pi loop appends the fenced block via --append-system-prompt) are the right shape for Claude-on-Pi and the wrong shape for open-weight-on-Pi unless spec 5 checks the model first; the park is defensible, but \"it may become moot\" is not the reason. Fetch does not make hand-condensation moot; it only changes the input to it.

Evidence auditorqualified
Strongest refutation

The citations P5 rests on all hold, but the argument built on them does not. (1) The one named precedent is misapplied: Codex's openai-docs skill (codex-rs/skills/src/assets/samples/openai-docs/SKILL.md, fetched 2026-09-24, line 36: "Use references/latest-model.md only as a disclosed fallback") is a documentation-lookup skill that answers user questions about OpenAI docs; it does not fetch model guidance to steer the agent. Codex's actual per-model steering is bundled models.json (~60KB per GPT-6 model, pack §6.3), i.e. vendor-authored per-model docs shipped by release, which is the thing P5 says to abandon. Its open issue #43164 (2026-09-06) shows fetch-first breaking offline users. (2) The fetched artifact is not a profile. Live word counts match the pack to the digit: Fable 5.1 6,610 words, Opus 5.5 3,969, best practices 8,013, migration guides 9,399 and 9,330. Of the Fable 5.1 guide's 16 H2 sections (fetched), about ten are API-only or off Joycraft's surface (effort levels, xhigh/max long outputs, vision crop/zoom, search triggering, safeguard false positives, lead-agent/subagent timing); the parked Opus 5.5 brief's own table scores 4 act / 2 handled by Claude Code / 5 not applicable. The pack's own inference (§6) concedes "the useful step is condensing a 2–9k-word vendor page into a ~1,000-word profile." Condensing is per-model authoring. Fetch removes the delivery step, not the labor, and the labor is where the value is. (3) "Static falls months behind" is Aider's number (5 months, §6.3), not Joycraft's. Joycraft tags: v0.7.11 09-03, v0.7.12 09-03, v0.7.13 09-06, v0.7.15 09-07, v0.7.16 09-23; the Fable 5.1 profile shipped 22 days after the 09-01 guide, and the Opus 5.5 feature was decomposed within two days of the 09-22 release. Joycraft's release cadence already matches Anthropic's ~3-week guide cadence, so the currency problem the fetch solves is not measured in this repo. (4) The maintainer's "push the new prompting guide to an update and everyone gets the new juice" is what the current design does: the profile is a vendor-owned template (docs/templates/reference/model-profile-claude-fable-5-1.md, ownership kind vendor per src/install-manifest.ts:30 as summarized in §8.8), replaced on `npx joycraft update` with a backup; PR #78 delivered it that way. Fetch adds nothing to "push to update." What survives is the subtract half: every vendor quote about removing stale instructions verified verbatim.

Qualification

P5 survives only as: bundled, condensed, versioned per-model profile delivered by `joycraft update` (today's mechanism) plus a subtract audit in optimize (vendor quotes verified), with fetch used strictly as a change detector against platform.claude.com/llms.txt and developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/latest-model.md that follows redirects, never constructs slugs for models not listed, and never places fetched vendor text into agent context unsummarized. The 'fetch beats per-model docs' framing is refuted; the 'subtract' framing stands.

On the human's position

The maintainer wrote: "I'm thinking that basically we can help this in the new system where all I have to do is push the new prompting guide to an update and everyone gets the new juice." Taken literally, that is already the shipped mechanism, not a new one: the Fable profile is a vendor-owned template replaced on `npx joycraft update` (src/model-profile.ts:14-24; CHANGELOG.md:37-40), and PR #78 delivered it exactly that way, 22 days after the guide. So the wish does not distinguish fetch from bundle; it distinguishes 'maintainer pushes' from 'user waits', and both designs are 'maintainer pushes'. What the maintainer may actually want is to skip the condensing step, and the evidence says that step is the product: the raw Fable 5.1 page is 6,610 words of which about ten of sixteen sections are off Joycraft's surface, and the parked brief's own audit found 5 of 11 Opus 5.5 sections not applicable. Pushing 'the new prompting guide' unsummarized pushes noise. My lens moves the position in one direction: keep 'push to update', keep the condensed per-model doc, and add fetch only as a currency signal (llms.txt or ETag says a guide changed or a new model has one) that opens the audit. The parking of the Opus 5.5 feature (Q3: 'it may become moot') is not supported by what I verified: nothing in the fetch design removes the work its nine specs do (tag blocks by model, swap the row, extract the unattended instruction, extend optimize's audit). Spec 8 (flag-thinking-rules-in-optimize) is the subtract half of P5 already written."

P6 · 5 skeptics

Jev routing on the hot path as a core part of the product

flip
Ruling

The maintainer's override — Jev routing prompts to skills, files, context-map pointers, and tool calls on the hot path, as a core part of the product, for anyone who brings a key — does not stand. It is replaced by: Jev ships as an opt-in, bring-your-own-key advisory judge off the hot path (doc ranking, report-claim verification over code-filtered state), plus a shadow-mode skill router that logs its pick beside the skill actually used; nothing touches the prompt path until an eval on Joycraft's own roster, with real prompts, shows Jev beating the model-free baselines, and files, context-map pointers, and tool calls stay out until each has its own measurement.

The claim as argued

The maintainer overrode the lead's advisory-first recommendation: Jev (TypeSafe) should route prompts to skills, files, context-map pointers, and tool calls on the hot path for anyone who brings a key, as a core part of the product, degrading to today's behavior when unreachable. Skeptic angles: the only routing evidence used 60-char descriptions and easy synthetic requests; a model-free forced-eval hook hit 22/22 with no false positives; hooks fail open; Jev reads literally and adversarial text moves its answer; hosted-only, US-only, no SLA, incidents on two of the last four days; per-user keys only under TypeSafe's terms; a zero-dependency CLI acquiring a hosted dependency on every prompt. The maintainer says it is "insanely good and basically free" in their own projects and is "open to the skeptics saying no."

Replacement claim

Jev is an optional, off-by-default, per-key advisory judge in Joycraft — off the hot path first (doc ranking, claim verification), shadow-logged as a skill router second — and becomes a hot-path router for skills only after a held-out eval on Joycraft's 22-skill roster with frontier agents beats the model-free forced-eval and disable-model-invocation baselines. It is never "core": a hosted, AS-IS, no-SLA dependency with recent latency incidents cannot be a product default, and file, context-map, and tool-call routing have no evidence anywhere.

Condition

Not a qualify ruling, but the exact path that revives a narrower P6 (all required): (a) a held-out invocation eval on Joycraft's actual roster (22 skills, or the post-P1 hub) with Fable 5.1 / Opus 5.5 as the agent and a Pi open-weight arm, using real prompts pulled from `joycraft telemetry` transcripts and labeled with the intended skill or "none", not prompts authored from the skills' own descriptions; (b) three arms — native description matching, disable-model-invocation on the 11 agent-entry skills plus a model-free forced-eval router block, and jev-1.13 — with Jev winning on wrong-load minus break-rate and on no-skill prompts; (c) any hot-path adapter carries its own client timeout of at most 2 s (the hook `timeout` field is settable) so a latency incident costs 2 s, not the 30 s default; (d) enabled per project on teams, not per developer, with every routing decision, confidence, and fallback written to the telemetry store; (e) TypeSafe confirms in writing that a developer running Joycraft's hook under their own key is an application "developed and operated by Customer" under the 2026-09-23 MCA; (f) skills only — files, context-map pointers, and tool calls stay off the hot path until each has its own eval.

Judge's reasoning

Four skeptics returned refuted and one (solo-pi) returned qualified, and the qualified return concedes the load-bearing words: "'Core part of the product' is refuted; 'an opt-in adapter that may help my model class' is not." So the panel is unanimous that "core" and "hot path" fail and disagrees only on what survives.

The proposition rests on one measurement and one anecdote. The measurement is TypeSafe's skill_suggestion cookbook, which every skeptic re-fetched and confirmed verbatim: Haiku 4.5 as agent, 182 skills, descriptions cut to 60 chars (Hermes's default, not TypeSafe's), 488 synthetic requests written by Sonnet 5 from each skill's own SKILL.md that the cookbook itself calls "easier than the ones users send", run on jev-1.12, thresholds tuned in-sample, wrong loads 16.8% to 7.3%, 37 fixed and 7 broken, and a conclusion the vendor scopes to "when an agent of yours carries a large roster". I verified the repo side: Joycraft has 22 skills with full descriptions totalling 3,619 chars (81 to 223 each), under the 8k listing budget, targeting frontier agents, with zero invocation evals (check.sh cannot assert which skill ran) and zero Jev references in src/, templates/, or scripts/. The regime does not transfer: the roster is 8x smaller, the descriptions 2 to 4x longer, the agent stronger, and P1 proposes to collapse the roster further, which removes the problem the cookbook solved. The only third-party Claude Code build of that cookbook (shimo4228/jev-skill-router, solo-pi) got 3 wrong of 6 on a real session and its README says it is "unlikely to help a strong model as a router". Meanwhile a model-free forced-eval hook measured 22/22 with 0/5 false positives while a Haiku classifier hook fired wrongly on 4/5 non-matching prompts (Spence, 2026-02-08, small n but the only direct comparison), and nobody has run either baseline on Joycraft's roster.

The anecdote ("insanely good and basically free" in the maintainer's own projects) has no artifact, number, task shape, or agent model, and the vendor's own coding-agents page positions Jev inside applications the agent builds, "not a drop-in replacement for the LLM behind Claude Code". Good-in-apps, where code retrieves and filters then asks a typed question over small state, is the inverse of a UserPromptSubmit hook shipping an unfiltered prompt plus 22 descriptions plus the active queue every turn; jev-1.13's own jaggedness page says "Accuracy falls as the state grows with content unrelated to the decision" and prescribes "Retrieve and filter in code first".

Three of the four routing targets (files, context-map pointers, tool calls) have no measurement anywhere in the pack, the repo, or TypeSafe's docs. Context-map routing has one destination today (a single Context Map row) and the map is never regenerated. Tool-call gating via PreToolUse adds latency, fails open by Anthropic's own words ("don't count on a stalled hook to act as a gate"), and the gated agent writes the input the judge reads.

"Degrades to today's behavior when unreachable" covers only the hard-outage case. The status page I fetched shows the Sep 23 incidents were latency (3 min and 12 min), not downtime; a latency incident does not trip the fail-open path, it stalls every prompt for every keyed colleague until the hook timeout (30 s default, though settable). The MCA, updated the day before the panel, is AS IS and AS AVAILABLE with no uptime commitment, and the JS SDK broke compatibility four days after release.

"Basically free" is true in dollars (about $0.042/M input, roughly $0.02/session) and false in the currencies a harness pays: latency on every prompt, a second vendor account and key per user, per-harness adapter maintenance on TypeSafe's cadence as well as Anthropic's, config-patch plumbing to reach about 15 existing installs, and on teams (team-lead) a per-developer fork in exactly the layer the maintainer's own Q1 answer says must stay invariant, with telemetry that cannot attribute a skill on Codex (src/telemetry.ts:404, verified). The maintainer's own list of wins (files, context-map pointers, research, web scraping, panels) is mostly the off-hot-path advisory use the lead recommended; only "help claude code with tool calls" needs the hot path, and that is the use with the weakest evidence and strongest adversarial exposure.

Why flip rather than qualify: the claim as written asserts three things — core, hot path, per-key default — and the evidence inverts all three. The condition field records the path back, but that path is the lead's advisory-first shape, which is the position the maintainer overrode. Why flip rather than kill: solo-pi's point survives — the one measured gain is on a mid-tier agent, which is exactly the open-weight Pi user class, and the inverted-U predicts those users benefit most; and off-hot-path uses match Jev's documented strengths. So Jev has a place in Joycraft; it is not the place the proposition names.

Strongest refutation considered

The strongest case for keeping was assembled from the skeptics' own evidence_against lists: the measured routing win is real and large (wrong loads more than halved); dollar cost is negligible; Claude Code's http hook handler with allowedEnvVars makes a per-user-key adapter thin and keeps the key out of the repo; the hook timeout field is settable so the stall can be capped at 1 to 2 s rather than 30 s; fail-open is real, so the worst case is today's behavior; the "zero-dependency CLI" premise is overstated (commander is a runtime dependency and the CLI already calls the npm registry behind a deadline); BYOK fits the MCA's "developed and operated by Customer" reading; inputs are not used for training; the forced-eval alternative is itself slower (10.7 s vs 6.4 s per prompt) and is prompt injection every turn; and for mid-tier open-weight agents the inverted-U predicts a real gain. I considered this seriously and it does defeat the weaker skeptic angles (cost, dependency purity, licensing as a hard blocker). It does not defeat the central one: none of it produces a measurement of Joycraft's own mis-route rate or of Jev's delta over a model-free baseline on this roster, and none of it touches files, context-map pointers, or tool calls, for which no evidence exists at all. A settable 2 s timeout and a compliant key make a good opt-in experiment, not a core default.

Human position moved?

Yes. The maintainer's Q5 position — Jev routing on the hot path, core, for anyone who brings a key, overriding the lead's advisory-first recommendation — was moved by all five skeptics and by my own verification, back to the lead's shape with three additions. The evidence that moved it: (1) the only routing measurement does not transfer (Haiku 4.5, 182 skills, 60-char Hermes-default index, synthetic Sonnet-5-authored requests the vendor calls easier than real ones, jev-1.12, 7 regressions) and Joycraft's regime is the opposite (22 skills, full descriptions, frontier agents, verified in-repo); (2) 'insanely good' has no artifact — zero Jev references in the repo, no eval, no numbers, no agent model — and comes from in-app use, which the vendor's coding-agents page and jaggedness page say is the correct shape while a per-prompt hook over unfiltered state is the shape they warn against; (3) three of the four named targets (files, context-map pointers, tool calls) have no measurement anywhere, and the context map has one row; (4) 'basically free' is true in dollars and false in latency (two of the last three incidents on the status page I fetched were latency, which does not trip fail-open), in complexity (per-harness adapter, per-user key plumbing, config-patch to ~15 installs, a moving SDK), and on teams in review variance (per-developer forks in the layer the maintainer's own Q1 says stays fixed, with Codex skill attribution unavailable); (5) the maintainer's own list of wins is mostly the off-hot-path advisory uses. What was not moved: the instinct that a typed judge is useful where a check needs meaning, and solo-pi's observation that the evidence favors mid-tier open-weight agents — the Pi user class — more than the frontier setup the maintainer tests on. The maintainer said he is open to the skeptics saying no; on 'core' and 'hot path' and 'for anyone who brings a key', this is that no. On 'Jev in Joycraft at all', it is not.

Skeptic disagreements

  • Status page reading: five skeptics gave five different incident lists and days-with-downtime counts (harness-expert: Sep 16, 19, 20, 22, two on Sep 23, 'no Sep 21 entry', 23 days; ai-researcher: Sep 20, 21, 22, 23, 18 days; solo-pi: eight events Sep 2, 7, 9, 16, 19, 20, 22, 23, 17 days; team-lead: Sep 21, 23, 24 plus console Sep 20-21; evidence-auditor: Sep 20-21, 22, 23-24, ~20 days). My fetch (page timestamp Sep 25 00:45 UTC) shows the rendered incident list as Sep 20 console, Sep 21 API 2 min, Sep 23 latency 3 min, Sep 23 latency+connection 12 min; API 99.827%. Harness-expert's 'no Sep 21 entry' is wrong; the extra dates others cite are not in the incident list and no days-with-downtime count was displayed. Direction (recent cluster, latency-type incidents) is unaffected.
  • Unit of enablement: harness-expert, solo-pi, and evidence-auditor accept per-user BYOK opt-in as the surviving shape; team-lead insists on per-project all-or-none because per-developer keys fork the path in the layer Q1 says stays invariant and telemetry cannot attribute skills on Codex. These are incompatible for a team install; my condition adopts team-lead's rule for teams.
  • Timeout ceiling: harness-expert says the 30 s UserPromptSubmit cap 'is the only ceiling Claude Code provides' and any adapter must carry its own sub-2 s client timeout; evidence-auditor says the hook entry's `timeout` field is settable, so Joycraft could cap the stall at 1-2 s in settings. The auditor's reading of the hooks doc is the more precise one; both agree the 30 s default is unacceptable.
  • Whether the MCA blocks the design: harness-expert says per-user keys are compliant and 'not a blocker'; team-lead says an org can be the Customer with employee Customer Users, so a team path exists; evidence-auditor demands written confirmation from TypeSafe before shipping; ai-researcher says the explicit key-sharing prohibition was not surfaced in its fetch while harness-expert and solo-pi quote §2.4 verbatim as present.
  • Who benefits: solo-pi argues the only measured gain is on a mid-tier agent (Haiku 4.5), so the maintainer's instinct is 'right for the wrong user' and open-weight Pi users would gain most, while offline Ollama users get nothing by construction; ai-researcher and harness-expert argue the frontier target means scaffolding benefit shrinks (arxiv 2609.20804) and the native error rate is plausibly already near Jev's 7.3% residual. Not contradictory, but they pull the surviving shape toward different harnesses.
  • The forced-eval baseline's cost: harness-expert notes it is slower (10.7 s vs 6.4 s per prompt) and is itself injection on every turn; ai-researcher, team-lead, and evidence-auditor treat it as the free zero-cost baseline. Solo-pi adds the always-loaded router block (Vercel 8KB index) as a second free baseline.
  • Cookbook information equality: team-lead alone notes Jev's second pass read up to 700 chars of each skill while the baseline agent kept 60-char lines, so the comparison is not information-equal; others treat the 60-char cut only as a non-transfer argument.
  • Fail-open semantics on Pi: solo-pi notes Pi `tool_call` can `return { block: true }` so a Pi gate does not fail open the way a Claude Code PreToolUse timeout does; harness-expert and evidence-auditor discuss only Claude Code semantics.
  • Description totals: harness-expert 3,931 chars (~180 each), ai-researcher/team-lead ~3.3k (79-221 each); my count is 3,619 (81-223). Differences come from counting the `description:` prefix; not load-bearing.
  • The '$0.042/M, 1,200 rpm, ~100 ms' claim: harness-expert and ai-researcher could not find it on api.md; solo-pi and evidence-auditor found price and rpm on models.md; all agree '~100 ms' appears nowhere in docs (homepage demo shows 0.114 s).
  • Whether 'imperative injected context can trigger prompt-injection defenses' is on the hooks page: ai-researcher says it is not; evidence-auditor says it is verbatim at line 1035. Unresolved; not load-bearing for P6.
  • Team-lead alone raises Vercel AI Gateway (providers typesafe-ai, digitalocean) as a possible team-key route with different terms; unverified by anyone.

  • Pack §7.5 'incidents Sep 21 and 23' actually matches the rendered incident list (my fetch), but understates: Sep 23 had two incidents and Sep 20 had a console outage. Harness-expert's 'no Sep 21 entry' is a misread; solo-pi's eight September events and team-lead's Sep 24 entry are not in the incident list as rendered.
  • Pack §7.4 'US-only hosting': found by no skeptic in the MCA, DPA (which references Ireland governing law and EU/UK/Swiss frameworks), models.md, or homepage; trust.typesafe.ai/subprocessors returned only its title (dead). Unsupported.
  • Pack §7.3 '~100 ms claimed': not on models.md or api.md; the homepage demo shows 'Completed in 0.114s' and cookbooks logged 0.09-0.31 s. Pricing and rpm live on models.md, not api.md as the pack implies.
  • Pack cited docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/skill-routing, which 404s; the live page is docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/skill_suggestion.md (team-lead).
  • Pack §7.6 omits material caveats present on the live cookbook page: run used jev-1.12 rendered 2026-07-31 (not 1.13); requests.json is proprietary; requests were synthetic, authored by Sonnet 5 from the skills' own SKILL.md; 0.30 thresholds appear tuned in-sample; the 60-char cut is Hermes's default; oracle floor 2.5%/1.2%; Jev's second pass read up to 700 chars while the baseline agent had 60; conclusion scoped to 'a large roster'.
  • Pack §7.8 under-reports jev-1.13 jaggedness: omits 'Accuracy falls as the state grows with content unrelated to the decision', unreliable counting, dates read as text, indirection weakness, and the 'filter in code first' mitigation.
  • Pack cites introduction/coding-agents.md only for 'what Jev is' and omits that page's actual guidance: Jev is for apps you build and 'not a drop-in replacement for the LLM behind Claude Code'.
  • Pack §2.10 (not load-bearing for P6): 'Stop hooks can't block' is a misread; the hooks page exit-code table lists Stop as 'Can block? Yes'. The pack's UNRESOLVED flag on P3 should resolve to yes.
  • Pack §7.9 'imperative injected context can trigger Claude's prompt-injection defenses': ai-researcher could not find it on the hooks page; evidence-auditor reports it verbatim at line 1035. Unresolved between skeptics.
  • The skeptic angle 'a zero-dependency CLI' in the task framing is overstated: commander is a runtime dependency and the CLI already makes a bounded, cached npm-registry call at SessionStart (src/update-check.ts:97, 311-329).
  • Pack §7 forced-eval citation omits that the forced-eval hook was slower (10.7 s vs 6.4 s per prompt) and that the false-positive set is n=5 across only 4 skills.
  • Ronacher 'less understandable while appearing more robust' (§1.8) and Superpowers dropping its Codex hook (§5.1): taken from the pack by harness-expert, not re-fetched by any skeptic.
  • SkillsBench (§4): pack cites the Feb 2026 abstract (86 tasks, +16.2pp); latest version says 87 tasks, +16.6pp. Minor, not load-bearing for P6.

What would change the ruling

A held-out invocation eval on Joycraft's own roster would move this ruling to qualify or keep: real prompts from the telemetry scanner labeled with the intended skill or 'none', three arms (native, disable-model-invocation plus model-free forced-eval router block, jev-1.13) on Fable 5.1 / Opus 5.5 and on a Pi open-weight agent, with Jev beating the best model-free arm on wrong-load minus break-rate and on no-skill and adversarial prompts by a stated margin. Any measurement at all of Jev routing files, context-map pointers, or tool calls in a coding agent would revive those targets individually. A 60-day status-page window with zero latency incidents, or a self-hosted/zero-retention option available below enterprise tier, would weaken the hot-path reliability objection. Written confirmation from TypeSafe that BYOK harness use fits 'developed and operated by Customer' under the 2026-09-23 MCA would remove the licensing hedge. A shadow-mode log across the ~15 colleague installs showing Jev's pick agreeing with the skill actually used at a rate above native matching would be the cheapest single piece of evidence to change the ruling.

Skeptics

Agent-harness expertrefuted
Strongest refutation

The only routing evidence fixes a problem Joycraft does not have. TypeSafe's cookbook improved skill selection for a 182-skill roster whose index Hermes truncates to 60 characters, in front of Haiku 4.5, on requests the cookbook itself says are "easier than the ones users send" — and it still left 7.3% wrong loads and broke 7 requests the agent had handled correctly alone (docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/skill_suggestion.md, fetched 2026-09-24). Joycraft has 22 skills, full descriptions totalling 3,931 chars (~180 each, src/skills/*.md), frontier agents, and nobody has measured its baseline mis-route rate. Where someone did measure a Claude Code skill-activation problem (Sonnet 4.5, 22 prompts), a model-free forced-eval hook went 50-55% → 22/22 with 0/5 false positives, while the model-classifier hook fired wrongly on 4/5 non-matching prompts (scottspence.com, 2026-02-08). Jev's own jaggedness page says "Accuracy falls as the state grows with content unrelated to the decision… Retrieve and filter in code first, and send only the fields the question needs" — the exact opposite of a per-prompt hook that ships prompt + 22 descriptions + active queue every turn. Putting a hosted call with three latency incidents in the last five days (status.typesafe.ai: Sep 19 downtime 18 min, Sep 20, Sep 22, two on Sep 23) in front of every prompt, for a gain no one has measured on this roster, and calling it core, is how harnesses accrete: each added defense makes the system "less understandable while appearing more robust" (Ronacher, pack §1.8). "Degrades to today's behavior when unreachable" covers the easy failure (hard outage → fast error). It does not cover the two failures a hot-path hook actually suffers: elevated latency (no error, every prompt waits, up to the 30 s UserPromptSubmit cap) and confident wrong answers (7.3% wrong loads, 7 regressions, adversarial text "can move the answer"). "Tool call" routing via PreToolUse adds 0.1–0.3 s per edit, fails open by Anthropic's own words ("don't count on a stalled hook to act as a gate"), and the gated agent authors the input. "Context-map pointers" routing has one destination today (AGENTS.md:189-191, a single row).

Qualification

Not applicable to the verdict as stated (refuted). What would survive: Jev as an opt-in, BYOK, off-hot-path advisory judge (doc ranking, claim verification over code-filtered state ≤32k), shipped only after (a) disable-model-invocation on the 11 agent-entry skills and (b) a model-free forced-eval router are measured on Joycraft's own 22-skill roster with frontier agents, and Jev shows a delta over that baseline on a held-out prompt set that includes adversarial and no-skill prompts. Any hot-path adapter must carry its own sub-2 s client timeout, since the 30 s UserPromptSubmit cap is the only ceiling Claude Code provides.

On the human's position

The maintainer: "ive been using it in projects and it's insanely good and basically free… it will help route what files to look at, what pointers in the context map to look at, help claude code with tool calls… it should be core part of the product now but I'm open to the skeptics saying no." My lens moves this, on three points. (1) Where the experience comes from. Using Jev in your own projects means Jev as an application primitive: code retrieves and filters, then asks a typed question over a small state — exactly what TypeSafe's programming model and its jaggedness page prescribe ("Retrieve and filter in code first"). A UserPromptSubmit hook is the inverse: an unfiltered prompt plus 22 descriptions plus the active queue on every turn, in front of a frontier agent that TypeSafe itself says Jev is "not a drop-in replacement for". Good-in-apps does not transfer to good-as-harness-router; the one published harness-routing result had a 60-char, 182-skill, Haiku-class problem Joycraft does not have and still regressed 7 requests. (2) "Basically free." True in dollars; false in the two currencies a harness pays. Latency: three elevated-latency incidents in the last five days, and a latency incident does not trip the fail-open path, it slows every prompt for every colleague with a key. Complexity: a per-harness hook adapter, per-user key plumbing, a moving SDK (breaking change four days after release), and config-patch machinery to reach the ~15 existing installs — all on the hot path, all to be maintained on TypeSafe's cadence as well as Anthropic's. (3) The three named targets. "Pointers in the context map": one row exists (AGENTS.md:189-191) and the map is never regenerated, so there is nothing to route until P0/P1 rebuild the pointer layer. "What files to look at": Jev needs code to enumerate ≤255 candidates first; the retrieval is the hard part and Jev only reranks it. "Help with tool calls": PreToolUse adds 0.1–0.3 s per edit, fails open, and the agent writes the input the judge reads. What does survive the maintainer's own words is the instinct behind them: a typed judge is useful where a check needs meaning. That is the lead's advisory-first shape — opt-in, off the hot path (doc ranking, claim verification), measured against the model-free forced-eval and disable-model-invocation baselines before anything touches a prompt. The override should be reversed; the enthusiasm should be pointed at a measurement, not a default.

AI researcherrefuted
Strongest refutation

There is no measurement of the thing the proposition claims to fix, and the one measurement that exists comes from a regime that does not transfer. The skill-suggestion cookbook (docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/skill_suggestion.md, fetched 2026-09-24) ran Haiku 4.5 over 182 Hermes skills with descriptions averaging 54 chars (max 60), on 488 synthetic single-turn prompts written by Sonnet 5 from the SKILL.md files, with the 0.30 gate/fit thresholds tuned on the same set and no held-out real-user prompts; the authors write that "the requests are easier than the ones users send." That is a deliberately starved baseline: a small agent, a roster 8x Joycraft's, descriptions 2–4x shorter than Joycraft's (79–221 chars, src/skills/*.md frontmatter; 3.3k total, under the 8k listing budget in claude-code#64606). Joycraft's condition is the opposite: 22 skills, full descriptions in budget, frontier agents (Fable 5.1 / Opus 5.5), and zero invocation evals (evidence pack §8.6: "No invocation evals; check.sh ... none checks which skill ran"). Even in the favorable regime Jev's residual wrong-load was 7.3% and it broke 7 of 488 requests the baseline got right; on a frontier model with 22 in-budget descriptions the native error rate is unmeasured and plausibly already near that residual, so a hot-path router can subtract as easily as add. The harness ablation (arxiv 2609.20804, 2026-09-17: "Planning shifts from an accuracy scaffold for weaker models to a cost saver for stronger models, with little change in accuracy") and Harness-Bench (stronger backends vary less across harnesses) predict exactly this shrinkage of scaffolding benefit, and §0 of the pack is itself the thesis that frontier models need less scaffolding — a per-prompt router is scaffolding. For three of the four routing targets (files, context-map pointers, tool calls) there is no measurement anywhere, and the vendor's own jaggedness page (jev-1.13.md, reviewed 2026-09-17) lists the properties those targets need — "Accuracy falls as the state grows with content unrelated to the decision", "does not count reliably", "reads dates as text", indirection "answered less reliably" — as weaknesses. A component with no baseline, no held-out delta, and a vendor sheet listing its failure modes on the exact inputs planned cannot be "core".

Qualification

Not the verdict, but the exact path that would revive a narrower P6: (1) build the invocation eval Joycraft lacks — real prompts from the maintainer's and colleagues' transcripts (src/telemetry.ts parsers), labeled with the intended skill or 'none', held out from any threshold tuning; (2) measure three arms on Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5: native description matching, a model-free router block/forced-eval hook, and Jev; (3) ship Jev skill routing — skills only — as per-user opt-in on the hot path only if its wrong-load minus break-rate beats the best model-free arm on the held-out set, with a kill criterion on the first month's telemetry; (4) files, context-map pointers, and tool calls stay off the hot path until each has its own eval; (5) 'core part of the product' is never available to a bring-your-own-key hosted dependency with no SLA and incidents on four of five recent days — 'optional, measured, off by default' is the ceiling the evidence supports.

Evidence for the refutation

  • Only routing evidence: Haiku 4.5, 182 skills, descriptions avg 54 / max 60 chars, 488 synthetic prompts by Sonnet 5, thresholds tuned in-sample, no held-out real prompts, authors admit requests are 'easier than the ones users send'; wrong-load 16.8%→7.3%, fixed 37 / broke 7, two calls per turn, 0.31s + 0.09–0.12s. https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/skill_suggestion.md (fetched 2026-09-24)
  • Joycraft has 22 skills with 79–221-char descriptions (~3.3k total) — a different regime from the cookbook's 60-char, 182-skill roster; no skill sets disable-model-invocation. /Users/compiler/Developer/joycraft/src/skills/*.md frontmatter (measured 2026-09-24); evidence pack §8.6, docs/research/2026-09-24-dynamic-joycraft-evidence.md:212
  • No invocation evals exist; check.sh grades output/file only, never which skill ran — so there is no baseline native-routing error rate for Joycraft to beat. docs/research/2026-09-24-dynamic-joycraft-evidence.md:212 (§8.6)
  • Vendor jaggedness sheet: literal reading; adversarial content 'can move the answer'; 'Accuracy falls as the state grows with content unrelated to the decision'; does not count reliably; dates read as text; indirection answered less reliably; score levels 'weak in numerical calibration'. https://docs.typesafe.ai/model-jaggedness/jev-1.13.md (last reviewed 2026-09-17, fetched 2026-09-24)
  • Confidence is a spread statistic, not a calibrated probability; no ECE, reliability diagram, or accuracy-at-threshold published; 'The correct threshold values depend on your domain and the performance of the model for your use case.' https://docs.typesafe.ai/confidence.md (fetched 2026-09-24)
  • Vendor positions Jev as a component inside applications the agent builds, not as a router for the coding agent; the coding-agents page makes no accuracy, latency, or reliability claims for hook use. https://docs.typesafe.ai/introduction/coding-agents.md (fetched 2026-09-24)
  • Scaffolding benefit shrinks with model strength: 'Planning shifts from an accuracy scaffold for weaker models to a cost saver for stronger models, with little change in accuracy.' https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20804 (submitted 2026-09-17)
  • Model-free alternative measured at 22/22 with 0 false positives (5/5 true negatives on harder set) on Sonnet 4.5 with 4 skills; Haiku classifier hook 22/22 but 4/5 false positives — an LLM judge on the hot path over-fires where a deterministic hook did not. https://scottspence.com/posts/measuring-claude-code-skill-activation-with-sandboxed-evals (2026-02-08, fetched 2026-09-24)
  • UserPromptSubmit default timeout 30s; a timed-out hook's output is discarded ('renders no decision'); a timed-out PreToolUse hook 'doesn't block the tool call ... don't count on a stalled hook to act as a gate'. https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks (fetched 2026-09-24)
  • API 99.827% 90-day uptime, 18 days with outages, incidents Sep 20, 21, 22 ('Elevated API latency'), 23 ('Elevated API latency', resolved Sep 24) — latency incidents are the failure mode that hits a 30s prompt hook. https://status.typesafe.ai (fetched 2026-09-24)
  • MCA: Services 'AS IS' and 'AS AVAILABLE'; TypeSafe 'may delete Customer Data at any time in its sole discretion'; 'may Process Telemetry without restriction'; Customer may not enable non-employees/non-contractors to use the Web Interface. https://typesafe.ai/legal/mca (effective 2026-09-23, fetched 2026-09-24)
  • Today the only network call in the product is a once-per-24h, 3s-deadline npm registry check; no UserPromptSubmit or http hook is installed. Hot-path Jev adds two hosted round-trips per prompt to a CLI whose sole runtime dependency is commander. /Users/compiler/Developer/joycraft/src/update-check.ts:19-20,97,327-331; /Users/compiler/Developer/joycraft/.claude/settings.json hooks block (SessionStart + PreToolUse only); package.json:42-44
  • Manifest has no ownership kind for a per-user key/config or Jev-generated routing state; kinds are vendor / create-once / config-patch only. /Users/compiler/Developer/joycraft/src/install-manifest.ts:174

Evidence against it

  • Retrieval over large rosters beats full-library prompting (Toollery; Anthropic tool search 79.5%→88.1%; Vercel 8KB index → 100%) — routing as a class has measured value when the roster is large. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22218 (2026-09-02); evidence pack §4.8 lines 122
  • Cost is not the constraint: ~$0.02/session vs ~$0.60 uncached Haiku; latency 0.2–0.6s per prompt is inside the 30s timeout. evidence pack §7 feasibility table, docs/research/2026-09-24-dynamic-joycraft-evidence.md:190-198
  • Fail-open design means the worst case is today's behavior, not a broken session — the downside is bounded if the adapter really does fail open. https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks (timeout semantics); docs/intent/2026-09-24-dynamic-joycraft.md:31
  • The maintainer reports strong first-hand results in their own projects ('insanely good and basically free'). evidence pack §10 Q5, docs/research/2026-09-24-dynamic-joycraft-evidence.md:271
  • Claude Code's `claude plugin eval` (tool_used grader, Δ vs no-plugin baseline) now exists, so the missing measurement is cheap to produce. evidence pack §2.9, docs/research/2026-09-24-dynamic-joycraft-evidence.md:56

The 'imperative injected context can trigger prompt-injection defenses' line (§7.9) is not on the hooks page.

Unverified

  • Joycraft's actual native mis-routing rate on Fable 5.1 / Opus 5.5 with its 22 descriptions — unmeasured by anyone; the whole proposition rests on it being high.
  • That any Jev routing over files, context-map pointers, or tool calls works at all — no cookbook, paper, or repo eval exists; only the vendor's own weaknesses list touches these inputs.
  • The maintainer's 'insanely good' — which projects, which use (in-app judgments per the vendor's coding-agents page, or as a Claude Code router?), any before/after numbers.
  • Cookbook figures on jev-1.12; whether 1.13 changed routing accuracy is not reported.
  • Explicit API-key-sharing prohibition in the MCA (the Web-Interface clause and §2.2 scope were confirmed; the key clause itself was not surfaced).
  • The pack's '$0.042 per million input tokens', '1,200 rpm', '64k tokens/request', 'US-only hosting' — none appear on api.md, confidence.md, or the MCA as fetched; source page not located.
  • Whether a Jev adapter for the http hook really fails open under partial responses (slow-but-not-timed-out, HTTP 429/529) rather than only on hard timeout.

On the human's position

The maintainer wrote: "ive been using it in projects and it's insanely good and basically free, it's too good that it should be a core part of the product as it will help route what files to look at, what pointers in the context map to look at, help claude code with tool calls, I think ti will speed up development and increase quality." From my lens every load-bearing word here is an inference from n=1 with no measured delta. "Insanely good" in the maintainer's projects is an in-application use — the vendor's own coding-agents page positions Jev inside apps the agent builds, not as a router for Claude Code — so the experience does not transfer to the claimed use. "Route what files ... what pointers ... tool calls" names three targets for which no measurement exists anywhere, and the vendor's jaggedness sheet lists the required properties (accuracy under large unrelated state, counting, dates, indirection) as known weaknesses. "Basically free" is true of dollars and false of the dependency: two hosted round-trips per prompt to a service that was in incident on four of the last five days (Sep 20–23, status.typesafe.ai) and whose contract says "AS AVAILABLE" and "may delete Customer Data at any time". "Speed up development" is asserted while the mechanism adds 0.2–0.6s per prompt and, during a latency incident, up to a 30s stall before the context is discarded. The one honest hedge — "I'm open to the skeptics saying no" — is the position I move to: no, as core and on the hot path, until the baseline is measured. The maintainer's confidence is not evidence; it is the hypothesis to test, and the test costs one afternoon with `claude plugin eval` (tool_used grader) plus real prompts pulled from the existing `joycraft telemetry` transcript scanner (src/telemetry.ts).

Solo dev on Pi, open-weight modelqualified
Strongest refutation

"Core part of the product" is refuted; "an opt-in adapter that may help my model class" is not. The only routing evidence (docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/skill_suggestion, fetched 2026-09-24) is on Haiku 4.5 over a 182-skill roster with 60-char descriptions and Sonnet-written requests the page itself calls "easier than the ones users send"; it fixed 37 and broke 7 of 488, and states a floor no router passes ("An agent given the right skill still does not always load it"). Joycraft ships 22 skills (src/skills/, 22 files) and P1 wants one hub, so the roster size the evidence assumes disappears. The one third-party Claude Code reference implementation of that cookbook (github.com/shimo4228/jev-skill-router, dated 2026-09-21) got 6/6 on scripted prompts and 3 wrong of 6 on a real session, added 0.7-1.6 s per prompt in inject mode, and its README says it is "unlikely to help a strong model as a router" because "The tokens spent on the skill listing do not go down by one." Routing to files, context-map pointers, and tool calls (the maintainer's actual pitch) has zero evidence anywhere in the pack or live docs; the only Jev ranking number is SEC-filing reranking top-1 5%->18%. Meanwhile the "free" service had eight September downtime/latency events (status.typesafe.ai, fetched 2026-09-24: Sep 2, 7, 9, 16, 19, 20, 22, 23), is "AS IS" with no SLA (typesafe.ai/legal/mca, effective Sep 23 2026), and rate limits "can change without notice" (docs.typesafe.ai/models.md). For a Pi user on Ollama (Pi docs models.md:19-27) the hot path is offline by construction, so "core" degrades to "today's behavior" for exactly the user my lens represents. A CLI whose whole runtime dependency list is `commander` (package.json:42-44) does not become a product whose default path calls a US-hosted API per prompt on one maintainer's unmeasured n=1.

Qualification

P6 survives only as: (1) opt-in, never default-on, gated behind a user-supplied key and an explicit local policy like update-check's; (2) shipped shadow-first on both Pi (`before_agent_start`) and Claude Code (UserPromptSubmit), logging Jev's pick beside the skill/file actually used, with inject mode enabled per harness only after the logged agreement rate on real prompts beats the zero-cost baseline (the model-free forced-eval / always-loaded router block, 22/22 on Spence's set, 100% on Vercel's 8KB index) on Joycraft's own ≤22-skill roster and on the target model class; (3) skill routing only — file, context-map, and tool-call routing stay out until any measurement exists; (4) the hard gates stay deterministic (path allowlists, exit codes), with Jev advisory, and on Pi `tool_call` blocking is allowed only for advisory-plus-confirm, never silent block; (5) the offline/local-model path (Ollama in models.json) is a first-class test case, not a degradation footnote, and the manifest gains an ownership kind for the key/policy file (src/install-manifest.ts:30 has none).

Evidence for the refutation

  • Routing evidence is synthetic, mid-roster-only, and self-caveated: jev-1.12, claude-haiku-4-5, 182 skills, 488 requests (315 covered), wrong loads 16.8%->7.3%, needless 9.8%->4.0%, 37 fixed / 7 broken; descriptions "truncated...to 60 characters by default"; covered requests "written by Claude Sonnet 5 from each skill's own SKILL.md" and "easier than the ones users send"; floor 2.5% wrong / 1.2% needless that "no selection method, however good, gets past". https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/skill_suggestion (fetched 2026-09-24)
  • Only Claude Code reference build of the cookbook: shadow-first UserPromptSubmit plugin; scripted 6/6 sensible (fit 0.93-0.98); real session 3 sensible / 3 wrong, wrong cases scored 0.34-0.64; inject-mode latency 0.7-1.6 s for six decisions; 21,597 input tokens in the example call; roster 50-59 skills; README: "unlikely to help a strong model as a router" and "The tokens spent on the skill listing do not go down by one." https://github.com/shimo4228/jev-skill-router (README dated 2026-09-21, fetched 2026-09-24)
  • A model-free forced-eval hook reached 100% (22/22) with 100% (5/5) true negatives; a Haiku classifier hook hit 22/22 but only 1/5 true negatives (4 false positives). Author caveat: the 22 cases are "straightforward" and "Real usage isn't that clean." A zero-cost, offline, deterministic baseline exists and was never measured against Jev on Joycraft's roster. https://scottspence.com/posts/measuring-claude-code-skill-activation-with-sandboxed-evals (2026-02-08, fetched 2026-09-24)
  • Independent reviewer of the cookbook: "I have not independently reproduced it"; "An extra model call is another cost and another opportunity to send the work in the wrong direction"; recommends adding a selector only "when recurring selection errors justify testing one, then compare the complete workflow with and without it." https://acdigest.substack.com/p/before-adding-more-skills-check-what (2026-09-24)
  • Reliability: eight September events on api.typesafe.ai (Sep 2: 3 min; Sep 7: 3 min; Sep 9: 6 min; Sep 16: 5 min; Sep 19: 18 min; Sep 20-21: API issues + console outage; Sep 22: elevated latency 12 min; Sep 23-24: elevated latency and connection issues). 90-day API uptime 99.827%. https://status.typesafe.ai (fetched 2026-09-24)
  • Terms: "THE SERVICES AND DOCUMENTATION ARE PROVIDED 'AS IS' AND 'AS AVAILABLE'"; "TYPESAFE DOES NOT WARRANT THAT CUSTOMER'S USE OF THE SERVICES WILL BE UNINTERRUPTED OR ERROR-FREE"; use is to "include the API into one or more software applications developed and operated by Customer for the benefit of Customer's end users"; "each Customer User keeps the Access Credentials confidential and does not share them with anyone else"; "TypeSafe may Process Telemetry without restriction". Effective date Sep 23, 2026, one day before this panel. https://typesafe.ai/legal/mca (effective 2026-09-23, fetched 2026-09-24)
  • Rate limits "250,000 tokens per second / 1,200 requests per minute" and "the limits above can change without notice"; no on-prem or self-hosted option; ZDR is enterprise-only. https://docs.typesafe.ai/models.md (fetched 2026-09-24)
  • Jev "answers the question you wrote, not the one you meant"; adversarial text "can move the answer"; "Accuracy falls as the state grows with content unrelated to the decision" — a router fed a 3-5k-token prompt+roster+queue state is exactly that shape. https://docs.typesafe.ai/model-jaggedness/jev-1.13.md (fetched 2026-09-24)
  • Pi users can run fully local models (Ollama/LM Studio/vLLM via models.json baseUrl http://localhost:11434/v1); for them a hosted router is unreachable by design and the 'core' feature is a no-op. node_modules/@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent/docs/models.md:19-27, providers.md:232
  • Joycraft's runtime dependency list is exactly one package (commander). The README's only existing network call is the update check: bounded, 24h-cached, "stays quiet when offline or unavailable" (README.md:79; src/update-check.ts:97, 312-329). Per-prompt hosted calls are a category change, not an extension of that pattern. package.json:42-44; README.md:79; src/update-check.ts:97,312-329
  • No manifest ownership kind exists for a hosted-dependency configuration or key (kinds are vendor | create-once | config-patch), and today's Pi extension registers only a /joycraft-next-spec command with no hooks — a hot-path router on Pi is a new surface, not a toggle. src/install-manifest.ts:30; .pi/extensions/joycraft-pipeline.ts:1-12,22-24
  • File/context-map/tool-call routing has no evidence: the pack's only non-skill ranking datum is 75-class SEC filings (confidence >=0.9 -> 90% right, rest 40%) and reranking top-1 5%->18%; no calibration metrics published. docs/research/2026-09-24-dynamic-joycraft-evidence.md:187 (section 7 item 7)

Evidence against it

  • The one measured gain is on a mid-tier model (Haiku 4.5), which is my model class; the inverted-U (Lin et al. 2605.30621: mid-tier benefits most) predicts a Qwen/Kimi agent gains more from an external router than a frontier one. The maintainer's intuition is closer to right for my user than for the Claude Code users he tested on. https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/skill_suggestion; docs/research/2026-09-24-dynamic-joycraft-evidence.md:116
  • Mechanically viable on Pi without Claude Code or MCP: `before_agent_start` "Can inject a message and/or modify the system prompt" and receives contextFiles and skills; `tool_call` can `return { block: true }`, so a Pi gate does not fail open the way a Claude Code PreToolUse timeout does. node_modules/@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent/docs/extensions.md:466-483, 69-73
  • Dollar cost is genuinely negligible: $0.042 per million input tokens, output free; two ~3-5k-token calls per prompt is under $0.001. Cookbook latency 0.16-0.31 s + 0.09-0.12 s per turn. https://docs.typesafe.ai/models.md; https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/skill_suggestion
  • Inputs are not used for training ("Jev is not trained on customer requests or responses"; MCA: will not include Customer Data in training datasets without consent), so the privacy objection for a solo dev is weaker than for a shared-key design. https://docs.typesafe.ai/models.md; https://typesafe.ai/legal/mca
  • Bring-your-own-key fits the MCA better than any shared-key design: the user is the Customer, the key stays with them, and the intent already commits to fail-open degradation. docs/intent/2026-09-24-dynamic-joycraft.md:31
